Linear Regression

This year the course ends with Linear Regression as Estimation (12 slides, all in the end-sem syllabus): fit a line y=β0+β1xy=\beta_0+\beta_1xy=β0​+β1​x by least squares, show that least squares is the maximum-likelihood estimate under Gaussian noise (and least absolute deviations under Laplace noise), find the MLE of the noise variance, the bias and MSE of β^0,β^1\hat\beta_0,\hat\beta_1β^​0​,β^​1​, and the Bayesian view (Gaussian prior gives penalised least squares; MAP and CE coincide). Regression was first examined in the 2026 surprise quiz (SQ26.1: MLEs of β∗\beta^*β∗ and σ2\sigma^2σ2 for regression through the origin, 10 of 40 marks); no 2022–25 paper asked it, and only five course questions exist, so this page leans on ProbabilityCourse and Bertsekas & Tsitsiklis problems at derivation level. Expect a derivation question: the normal equations, LS = ML, unbiasedness and variance of the slope, or the n−2n-2n−2 variance estimate. The linear LMS problems of section 4 go slightly beyond the slides (the boundary rules put linear LMS here); do them last.

Must-do first

★ Past paper: SQ26.1 (2026 Surprise Quiz Q1). Then the most exam-likely questions:

1 · Least squares: T26-14.5 · PCS8.5.5.3
2 · Least squares as ML: T26-14.6 · PCS8.5.5.5
3 · Sampling properties: H26-12.1 · H25-11.7 · BT9.19
4 · Bayesian view and linear LMS: BT8.14 · BT8.22

Only SQ26.1 is a past-paper question, so only it carries the ★ Must-do chip.

What is inside

    1  The model and least squares · slides 2–5

    Theory recap
    The model (slide 2)

    Data: pairs (x1,y1),…,(xn,yn)(x_1,y_1),\dots,(x_n,y_n)(x1​,y1​),…,(xn​,yn​). Model: Yi=β0∗+β1∗xi+εiY_i=\beta_0^*+\beta_1^*x_i+\varepsilon_iYi​=β0∗​+β1∗​xi​+εi​ with β0∗,β1∗\beta_0^*,\beta_1^*β0∗​,β1∗​ unknown and noise ε1,…,εn\varepsilon_1,\dots,\varepsilon_nε1​,…,εn​ i.i.d., independent of the xix_ixi​, E[εi]=0E[\varepsilon_i]=0E[εi​]=0, Var⁡(εi)=σ2\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_i)=\sigma^2Var(εi​)=σ2. So E[Yi∣Xi=xi]=β0∗+β1∗xiE[Y_i\mid X_i=x_i]=\beta_0^*+\beta_1^*x_iE[Yi​∣Xi​=xi​]=β0∗​+β1∗​xi​ and Var⁡(Yi∣Xi=xi)=σ2\operatorname{Var}(Y_i\mid X_i=x_i)=\sigma^2Var(Yi​∣Xi​=xi​)=σ2.

    Least squares (slides 3–4)

    Residual of a candidate line: ei=yi−β0−β1xie_i=y_i-\beta_0-\beta_1x_iei​=yi​−β0​−β1​xi​. Least squares minimises J(β0,β1)=∑i=1nei2=∑i=1n(yi−β0−β1xi)2.J(\beta_0,\beta_1)=\sum_{i=1}^n e_i^2=\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i-\beta_0-\beta_1x_i)^2 .J(β0​,β1​)=i=1∑n​ei2​=i=1∑n​(yi​−β0​−β1​xi​)2. Setting both partial derivatives to zero gives the normal equations ∂J∂β0=−2∑i(yi−β0−β1xi)=0,∂J∂β1=−2∑ixi(yi−β0−β1xi)=0.\frac{\partial J}{\partial\beta_0}=-2\sum_i (y_i-\beta_0-\beta_1x_i)=0,\qquad \frac{\partial J}{\partial\beta_1}=-2\sum_i x_i(y_i-\beta_0-\beta_1x_i)=0 .∂β0​∂J​=−2i∑​(yi​−β0​−β1​xi​)=0,∂β1​∂J​=−2i∑​xi​(yi​−β0​−β1​xi​)=0. The first, divided by −2n-2n−2n, gives β0=yˉ−β1xˉ\beta_0=\bar y-\beta_1\bar xβ0​=yˉ​−β1​xˉ.

    The estimates (slide 5)

    With Sxx=∑i(xi−xˉ)2S_{xx}=\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2Sxx​=∑i​(xi​−xˉ)2 and Sxy=∑i(xi−xˉ)(yi−yˉ)S_{xy}=\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y)Sxy​=∑i​(xi​−xˉ)(yi​−yˉ​): β^1=SxySxx,β^0=yˉ−β^1xˉ.\hat\beta_1=\frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}},\qquad \hat\beta_0=\bar y-\hat\beta_1\bar x .β^​1​=Sxx​Sxy​​,β^​0​=yˉ​−β^​1​xˉ. Derivation of the slope: put β0=yˉ−β1xˉ\beta_0=\bar y-\beta_1\bar xβ0​=yˉ​−β1​xˉ into the second equation: ∑ixici=0\sum_i x_ic_i=0∑i​xi​ci​=0 with ci=(yi−yˉ)−β1(xi−xˉ)c_i=(y_i-\bar y)-\beta_1(x_i-\bar x)ci​=(yi​−yˉ​)−β1​(xi​−xˉ). Since ∑ici=0\sum_i c_i=0∑i​ci​=0, also ∑ixˉci=0\sum_i\bar x c_i=0∑i​xˉci​=0; subtracting, ∑i(xi−xˉ)ci=0\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)c_i=0∑i​(xi​−xˉ)ci​=0, i.e. Sxy=β1SxxS_{xy}=\beta_1S_{xx}Sxy​=β1​Sxx​. Useful identities: ∑i(xi−xˉ)=0\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)=0∑i​(xi​−xˉ)=0, Sxy=∑i(xi−xˉ)yiS_{xy}=\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)y_iSxy​=∑i​(xi​−xˉ)yi​, Sxx=∑ixi2−nxˉ2S_{xx}=\sum_i x_i^2-n\bar x^2Sxx​=∑i​xi2​−nxˉ2.

    Residuals of the fitted line

    With y^i=β^0+β^1xi\hat y_i=\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1x_iy^​i​=β^​0​+β^​1​xi​ and ei=yi−y^ie_i=y_i-\hat y_iei​=yi​−y^​i​, the normal equations say exactly ∑iei=0,∑ixiei=0,hence∑iy^iei=0.\sum_i e_i=0,\qquad \sum_i x_ie_i=0,\qquad\text{hence}\quad \sum_i\hat y_ie_i=0 .i∑​ei​=0,i∑​xi​ei​=0,hencei∑​y^​i​ei​=0. Also yˉ=β^0+β^1xˉ\bar y=\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1\bar xyˉ​=β^​0​+β^​1​xˉ: the fitted line passes through (xˉ,yˉ)(\bar x,\bar y)(xˉ,yˉ​).

    R2R^2R2 (beyond the slides: PC §8.5.2)

    With Syy=∑i(yi−yˉ)2S_{yy}=\sum_i(y_i-\bar y)^2Syy​=∑i​(yi​−yˉ​)2: r2=Sxy2SxxSyy∈[0,1]r^2=\dfrac{S_{xy}^2}{S_{xx}S_{yy}}\in[0,1]r2=Sxx​Syy​Sxy2​​∈[0,1]. Because the residuals are orthogonal to the fitted values, ∑(yi−yˉ)2⏟SST=∑(y^i−yˉ)2⏟SSR+∑ei2⏟SSE\underbrace{\textstyle\sum(y_i-\bar y)^2}_{\text{SST}}=\underbrace{\textstyle\sum(\hat y_i-\bar y)^2}_{\text{SSR}}+\underbrace{\textstyle\sum e_i^2}_{\text{SSE}}SST∑(yi​−yˉ​)2​​=SSR∑(y^​i​−yˉ​)2​​+SSE∑ei2​​​, so r2=SSR/SST=1−SSE/SSTr^2=\text{SSR}/\text{SST}=1-\text{SSE}/\text{SST}r2=SSR/SST=1−SSE/SST: the share of the variation in yyy explained by the line. It is the sample version of ρ2=β12Var⁡(X)/Var⁡(Y)=Cov⁡(X,Y)2/(Var⁡XVar⁡Y)\rho^2=\beta_1^2\operatorname{Var}(X)/\operatorname{Var}(Y)=\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)^2/(\operatorname{Var}X\operatorname{Var}Y)ρ2=β12​Var(X)/Var(Y)=Cov(X,Y)2/(VarXVarY).

    Watch out

    ∑ei=0\sum e_i=0∑ei​=0 comes from the ∂J/∂β0\partial J/\partial\beta_0∂J/∂β0​ equation. A model without an intercept has no such equation, and its residuals need not sum to zero (see T26-14.6). And r2=1r^2=1r2=1 with two points means nothing: two points always lie on a line.

    (Least Squares Estimation) Consider a dataset consisting of n=4n=4n=4 observations: (x1,y1)=(1,2)(x_1,y_1)=(1,2)(x1​,y1​)=(1,2), (x2,y2)=(2,4)(x_2,y_2)=(2,4)(x2​,y2​)=(2,4), (x3,y3)=(3,5)(x_3,y_3)=(3,5)(x3​,y3​)=(3,5), and (x4,y4)=(4,7)(x_4,y_4)=(4,7)(x4​,y4​)=(4,7).     1. Compute the sample means xˉ\bar xxˉ and yˉ\bar yyˉ​.

    PCS8.5.5.1Fit, fitted values, residuals and R2R^2R2 PC §8.5.5 Solved Problem 1
    Consider the following observed values of (xi,yi)(x_i,y_i)(xi​,yi​): (−1,6), (0,3), (1,2), (2,−1)(-1,6),\ (0,3),\ (1,2),\ (2,-1)(−1,6), (0,3), (1,2), (2,−1).
    1. Find the estimated regression line y^=β^0+β^1x\hat y=\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1xy^​=β^​0​+β^​1​x based on the observed data.
    2. For each xix_ixi​, compute the fitted value of yiy_iyi​ using y^i=β^0+β^1xi\hat y_i=\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1x_iy^​i​=β^​0​+β^​1​xi​.
    3. Compute the residuals, ei=yi−y^ie_i=y_i-\hat y_iei​=yi​−y^​i​.
    4. Find RRR-squared (the coefficient of determination).

    Same drill as PC §8.6 Problem 21 and B&T Ch. 9 Problem 16 (not listed separately).

    Solution · follows ProbabilityCourse's solution

    (a) The line

    xˉ=−1+0+1+24=0.5,yˉ=6+3+2−14=2.5,\bar x=\frac{-1+0+1+2}{4}=0.5,\qquad \bar y=\frac{6+3+2-1}{4}=2.5,xˉ=4−1+0+1+2​=0.5,yˉ​=46+3+2−1​=2.5, Sxx=(−1.5)2+(−0.5)2+0.52+1.52=5,S_{xx}=(-1.5)^2+(-0.5)^2+0.5^2+1.5^2=5,Sxx​=(−1.5)2+(−0.5)2+0.52+1.52=5, Sxy=(−1.5)(3.5)+(−0.5)(0.5)+(0.5)(−0.5)+(1.5)(−3.5)=−11.S_{xy}=(-1.5)(3.5)+(-0.5)(0.5)+(0.5)(-0.5)+(1.5)(-3.5)=-11 .Sxy​=(−1.5)(3.5)+(−0.5)(0.5)+(0.5)(−0.5)+(1.5)(−3.5)=−11. β^1=SxySxx=−2.2,β^0=yˉ−β^1xˉ=2.5+2.2(0.5)=3.6.\hat\beta_1=\frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}}=-2.2,\qquad \hat\beta_0=\bar y-\hat\beta_1\bar x=2.5+2.2(0.5)=3.6 .β^​1​=Sxx​Sxy​​=−2.2,β^​0​=yˉ​−β^​1​xˉ=2.5+2.2(0.5)=3.6.

    (b) Fitted values

    y^i=3.6−2.2xi\hat y_i=3.6-2.2x_iy^​i​=3.6−2.2xi​: y^1=5.8, y^2=3.6, y^3=1.4, y^4=−0.8\hat y_1=5.8,\ \hat y_2=3.6,\ \hat y_3=1.4,\ \hat y_4=-0.8y^​1​=5.8, y^​2​=3.6, y^​3​=1.4, y^​4​=−0.8.

    (c) Residuals

    e1=0.2, e2=−0.6, e3=0.6, e4=−0.2e_1=0.2,\ e_2=-0.6,\ e_3=0.6,\ e_4=-0.2e1​=0.2, e2​=−0.6, e3​=0.6, e4​=−0.2 (they sum to 0).

    (d) R2R^2R2

    Syy=3.52+0.52+(−0.5)2+(−3.5)2=25,r2=Sxy2SxxSyy=1215⋅25=0.968.S_{yy}=3.5^2+0.5^2+(-0.5)^2+(-3.5)^2=25,\qquad r^2=\frac{S_{xy}^2}{S_{xx}S_{yy}}=\frac{121}{5\cdot25}=0.968 .Syy​=3.52+0.52+(−0.5)2+(−3.5)2=25,r2=Sxx​Syy​Sxy2​​=5⋅25121​=0.968.

    Check: SSE=0.04+0.36+0.36+0.04=0.8\text{SSE}=0.04+0.36+0.36+0.04=0.8SSE=0.04+0.36+0.36+0.04=0.8 and 1−SSE/Syy=1−0.8/25=0.9681-\text{SSE}/S_{yy}=1-0.8/25=0.9681−SSE/Syy​=1−0.8/25=0.968.

    PCS8.5.5.3The three residual identities PC §8.5.5 Solved Problem 3
    Show that, in a simple linear regression, the estimated coefficients β^0\hat\beta_0β^​0​ and β^1\hat\beta_1β^​1​ (least squares estimates of β0\beta_0β0​ and β1\beta_1β1​) satisfy the following equations ∑i=1nei=0,∑i=1neixi=0,∑i=1neiy^i=0,\sum_{i=1}^n e_i=0,\qquad \sum_{i=1}^n e_ix_i=0,\qquad \sum_{i=1}^n e_i\hat y_i=0,i=1∑n​ei​=0,i=1∑n​ei​xi​=0,i=1∑n​ei​y^​i​=0, where ei=yi−y^i=yi−β^0−β^1xie_i=y_i-\hat y_i=y_i-\hat\beta_0-\hat\beta_1x_iei​=yi​−y^​i​=yi​−β^​0​−β^​1​xi​. Hint: β^0\hat\beta_0β^​0​ and β^1\hat\beta_1β^​1​ satisfy the two equations obtained by setting the partial derivatives of the sum of squared errors to zero. By cancelling the (−2)(-2)(−2) factor, you can write ∑i(yi−β^0−β^1xi)=0\sum_i(y_i-\hat\beta_0-\hat\beta_1x_i)=0∑i​(yi​−β^​0​−β^​1​xi​)=0 and ∑i(yi−β^0−β^1xi)xi=0\sum_i(y_i-\hat\beta_0-\hat\beta_1x_i)x_i=0∑i​(yi​−β^​0​−β^​1​xi​)xi​=0.
    Solution · follows ProbabilityCourse's solution

    (β^0,β^1)(\hat\beta_0,\hat\beta_1)(β^​0​,β^​1​) minimises J(β0,β1)=∑i(yi−β0−β1xi)2J(\beta_0,\beta_1)=\sum_i(y_i-\beta_0-\beta_1x_i)^2J(β0​,β1​)=∑i​(yi​−β0​−β1​xi​)2, a differentiable function, so both partial derivatives vanish there:

    ∂J∂β0∣β^=−2∑i(yi−β^0−β^1xi)=0,∂J∂β1∣β^=−2∑i(yi−β^0−β^1xi)xi=0.\frac{\partial J}{\partial\beta_0}\Big|_{\hat\beta}=-2\sum_i(y_i-\hat\beta_0-\hat\beta_1x_i)=0,\qquad \frac{\partial J}{\partial\beta_1}\Big|_{\hat\beta}=-2\sum_i(y_i-\hat\beta_0-\hat\beta_1x_i)x_i=0 .∂β0​∂J​​β^​​=−2i∑​(yi​−β^​0​−β^​1​xi​)=0,∂β1​∂J​​β^​​=−2i∑​(yi​−β^​0​−β^​1​xi​)xi​=0.

    Cancel −2-2−2 and use ei=yi−β^0−β^1xie_i=y_i-\hat\beta_0-\hat\beta_1x_iei​=yi​−β^​0​−β^​1​xi​:

    ∑iei=0,∑ieixi=0.\sum_i e_i=0,\qquad \sum_i e_ix_i=0 .i∑​ei​=0,i∑​ei​xi​=0.

    For the third, expand y^i\hat y_iy^​i​ and use linearity of the sum:

    ∑ieiy^i=∑iei(β^0+β^1xi)=β^0∑iei+β^1∑ieixi=0+0=0.\sum_i e_i\hat y_i=\sum_i e_i(\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1x_i)=\hat\beta_0\sum_i e_i+\hat\beta_1\sum_i e_ix_i=0+0=0 .i∑​ei​y^​i​=i∑​ei​(β^​0​+β^​1​xi​)=β^​0​i∑​ei​+β^​1​i∑​ei​xi​=0+0=0.
    Answer

    ∑ei=0\sum e_i=0∑ei​=0, ∑eixi=0\sum e_ix_i=0∑ei​xi​=0 are the two normal equations; ∑eiy^i=β^0∑ei+β^1∑eixi=0\sum e_i\hat y_i=\hat\beta_0\sum e_i+\hat\beta_1\sum e_ix_i=0∑ei​y^​i​=β^​0​∑ei​+β^​1​∑ei​xi​=0. Geometrically: the residual vector is orthogonal to 1\mathbf 11, to x\mathbf xx, and so to every fitted vector.

    PCS8.5.5.4R2R^2R2 as explained over total variation PC §8.5.5 Solved Problem 4
    Show that the coefficient of determination can also be obtained as r2=∑i=1n(y^i−yˉ)2∑i=1n(yi−yˉ)2.r^2=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n(\hat y_i-\bar y)^2}{\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-\bar y)^2}.r2=∑i=1n​(yi​−yˉ​)2∑i=1n​(y^​i​−yˉ​)2​. (Here r2=Sxy2/(SxxSyy)r^2=S_{xy}^2/(S_{xx}S_{yy})r2=Sxy2​/(Sxx​Syy​) with Syy=∑i(yi−yˉ)2S_{yy}=\sum_i(y_i-\bar y)^2Syy​=∑i​(yi​−yˉ​)2.)
    Solution · follows ProbabilityCourse's solution

    The fitted values are y^i=β^0+β^1xi\hat y_i=\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1x_iy^​i​=β^​0​+β^​1​xi​, and since β^0=yˉ−β^1xˉ\hat\beta_0=\bar y-\hat\beta_1\bar xβ^​0​=yˉ​−β^​1​xˉ, the line passes through the means: yˉ=β^0+β^1xˉ\bar y=\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1\bar xyˉ​=β^​0​+β^​1​xˉ. Subtracting,

    y^i−yˉ=β^1(xi−xˉ).\hat y_i-\bar y=\hat\beta_1(x_i-\bar x).y^​i​−yˉ​=β^​1​(xi​−xˉ).

    So

    ∑i(y^i−yˉ)2=β^12∑i(xi−xˉ)2=β^12Sxx.\sum_i(\hat y_i-\bar y)^2=\hat\beta_1^2\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2=\hat\beta_1^2S_{xx}.i∑​(y^​i​−yˉ​)2=β^​12​i∑​(xi​−xˉ)2=β^​12​Sxx​.

    Divide by SyyS_{yy}Syy​ and use β^1=Sxy/Sxx\hat\beta_1=S_{xy}/S_{xx}β^​1​=Sxy​/Sxx​:

    ∑i(y^i−yˉ)2∑i(yi−yˉ)2=β^12SxxSyy=Sxy2Sxx2⋅SxxSyy=Sxy2SxxSyy=r2.\frac{\sum_i(\hat y_i-\bar y)^2}{\sum_i(y_i-\bar y)^2}=\frac{\hat\beta_1^2S_{xx}}{S_{yy}}=\frac{S_{xy}^2}{S_{xx}^2}\cdot\frac{S_{xx}}{S_{yy}}=\frac{S_{xy}^2}{S_{xx}S_{yy}}=r^2 .∑i​(yi​−yˉ​)2∑i​(y^​i​−yˉ​)2​=Syy​β^​12​Sxx​​=Sxx2​Sxy2​​⋅Syy​Sxx​​=Sxx​Syy​Sxy2​​=r2.

    (ProbabilityCourse writes β0,β1\beta_0,\beta_1β0​,β1​ for the estimates here; they must be the least-squares values, since yˉ=β^0+β^1xˉ\bar y=\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1\bar xyˉ​=β^​0​+β^​1​xˉ holds only for them.) Combined with SST=SSR+SSE\text{SST}=\text{SSR}+\text{SSE}SST=SSR+SSE (cross term 2∑iei(y^i−yˉ)=2∑eiy^i−2yˉ∑ei=02\sum_i e_i(\hat y_i-\bar y)=2\sum e_i\hat y_i-2\bar y\sum e_i=02∑i​ei​(y^​i​−yˉ​)=2∑ei​y^​i​−2yˉ​∑ei​=0 by PCS8.5.5.3), this also gives r2=1−SSE/SST∈[0,1]r^2=1-\text{SSE}/\text{SST}\in[0,1]r2=1−SSE/SST∈[0,1].

    Answer

    ∑(y^i−yˉ)2=β^12Sxx=Sxy2/Sxx\sum(\hat y_i-\bar y)^2=\hat\beta_1^2S_{xx}=S_{xy}^2/S_{xx}∑(y^​i​−yˉ​)2=β^​12​Sxx​=Sxy2​/Sxx​, so the ratio equals Sxy2/(SxxSyy)=r2S_{xy}^2/(S_{xx}S_{yy})=r^2Sxy2​/(Sxx​Syy​)=r2.

    PCS8.5.5.2Population variance decomposition PC §8.5.5 Solved Problem 2
    Consider the model Y=β0+β1X+ϵY=\beta_0+\beta_1X+\epsilonY=β0​+β1​X+ϵ, where ϵ\epsilonϵ is a N(0,σ2)N(0,\sigma^2)N(0,σ2) random variable independent of XXX. Let also Y^=β0+β1X\hat Y=\beta_0+\beta_1XY^=β0​+β1​X. Show that E[(Y−EY)2]=E[(Y^−EY)2]+E[(Y−Y^)2].E[(Y-EY)^2]=E[(\hat Y-EY)^2]+E[(Y-\hat Y)^2].E[(Y−EY)2]=E[(Y^−EY)2]+E[(Y−Y^)2].
    Solution · follows ProbabilityCourse's solution

    Since XXX and ϵ\epsilonϵ are independent, they are uncorrelated, so

    Var⁡(Y)=Var⁡(β1X+ϵ)=β12Var⁡(X)+Var⁡(ϵ).\operatorname{Var}(Y)=\operatorname{Var}(\beta_1X+\epsilon)=\beta_1^2\operatorname{Var}(X)+\operatorname{Var}(\epsilon).Var(Y)=Var(β1​X+ϵ)=β12​Var(X)+Var(ϵ).

    Take expectations in the model: EY=β0+β1EX+Eϵ=β0+β1EXEY=\beta_0+\beta_1EX+E\epsilon=\beta_0+\beta_1EXEY=β0​+β1​EX+Eϵ=β0​+β1​EX. Hence

    Y^−EY=(β0+β1X)−(β0+β1EX)=β1(X−EX) ⇒ E[(Y^−EY)2]=β12Var⁡(X).\hat Y-EY=(\beta_0+\beta_1X)-(\beta_0+\beta_1EX)=\beta_1(X-EX)\ \Rightarrow\ E[(\hat Y-EY)^2]=\beta_1^2\operatorname{Var}(X).Y^−EY=(β0​+β1​X)−(β0​+β1​EX)=β1​(X−EX) ⇒ E[(Y^−EY)2]=β12​Var(X).

    Also E[(Y−EY)2]=Var⁡(Y)E[(Y-EY)^2]=\operatorname{Var}(Y)E[(Y−EY)2]=Var(Y) and Y−Y^=ϵY-\hat Y=\epsilonY−Y^=ϵ, so E[(Y−Y^)2]=E[ϵ2]=Var⁡(ϵ)E[(Y-\hat Y)^2]=E[\epsilon^2]=\operatorname{Var}(\epsilon)E[(Y−Y^)2]=E[ϵ2]=Var(ϵ) (as Eϵ=0E\epsilon=0Eϵ=0). Substituting into the first line gives the identity.

    Answer

    Var⁡(Y)=β12Var⁡(X)+σ2\operatorname{Var}(Y)=\beta_1^2\operatorname{Var}(X)+\sigma^2Var(Y)=β12​Var(X)+σ2: total variance = explained part E[(Y^−EY)2]E[(\hat Y-EY)^2]E[(Y^−EY)2] + error part E[(Y−Y^)2]E[(Y-\hat Y)^2]E[(Y−Y^)2]. The explained share β12Var⁡X/Var⁡Y=ρ2\beta_1^2\operatorname{Var}X/\operatorname{Var}Y=\rho^2β12​VarX/VarY=ρ2 is what r2r^2r2 estimates.

    PC8.6.22Two points: a perfect but meaningless fit PC §8.6 Problem 22
    Consider the following observed values of (xi,yi)(x_i,y_i)(xi​,yi​): (1,3), (3,7)(1,3),\ (3,7)(1,3), (3,7).
    1. Find the estimated regression line y^=β^0+β^1x\hat y=\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1xy^​=β^​0​+β^​1​x based on the observed data.

    Solution · written for this guide

    (a)

    xˉ=2, yˉ=5,Sxx=(−1)2+12=2,Sxy=(−1)(−2)+(1)(2)=4,\bar x=2,\ \bar y=5,\quad S_{xx}=(-1)^2+1^2=2,\quad S_{xy}=(-1)(-2)+(1)(2)=4,xˉ=2, yˉ​=5,Sxx​=(−1)2+12=2,Sxy​=(−1)(−2)+(1)(2)=4, β^1=42=2,β^0=5−2⋅2=1,y^=1+2x.\hat\beta_1=\frac{4}{2}=2,\qquad \hat\beta_0=5-2\cdot2=1,\qquad \hat y=1+2x .β^​1​=24​=2,β^​0​=5−2⋅2=1,y^​=1+2x.

    (b), (c)

    y^1=3, y^2=7\hat y_1=3,\ \hat y_2=7y^​1​=3, y^​2​=7; residuals e1=e2=0e_1=e_2=0e1​=e2​=0.

    (d)

    Syy=(−2)2+22=8S_{yy}=(-2)^2+2^2=8Syy​=(−2)2+22=8, r2=162⋅8=1r^2=\dfrac{16}{2\cdot 8}=1r2=2⋅816​=1.

    (e)

    Two points with different xxx always lie exactly on one line, so J=0J=0J=0 and r2=1r^2=1r2=1 for any data of this size: the fit carries no evidence about the model. There are two parameters and two observations, so nothing is left to estimate the noise: SSE=0\text{SSE}=0SSE=0 and the unbiased estimate SSE/(n−2)\text{SSE}/(n-2)SSE/(n−2) is 0/00/00/0, undefined. We cannot conclude the line is a good model; we need n>2n>2n>2 points.

    Answer

    y^=1+2x\hat y=1+2xy^​=1+2x, fitted values 3,73,73,7, residuals 0,00,00,0, r2=1r^2=1r2=1; but with n=2n=2n=2 a perfect fit is automatic, so it says nothing about the quality of the model.

    2  Least squares as maximum likelihood · slides 6–8

    Theory recap
    LS is the MLE under Gaussian noise (slide 6)

    If εi∼N(0,σ2)\varepsilon_i\sim N(0,\sigma^2)εi​∼N(0,σ2) i.i.d., then given the xix_ixi​ the YiY_iYi​ are independent with Yi∼N(β0+β1xi,σ2)Y_i\sim N(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i,\sigma^2)Yi​∼N(β0​+β1​xi​,σ2), so L(y1,…,yn;β0,β1)=∏i=1n12πσ2exp⁡ ⁣(−(yi−β0−β1xi)22σ2),ln⁡L=−n2ln⁡(2πσ2)−12σ2J(β0,β1).L(y_1,\dots,y_n;\beta_0,\beta_1)=\prod_{i=1}^n\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}\exp\!\Big(-\frac{(y_i-\beta_0-\beta_1x_i)^2}{2\sigma^2}\Big),\qquad \ln L=-\frac n2\ln(2\pi\sigma^2)-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}J(\beta_0,\beta_1).L(y1​,…,yn​;β0​,β1​)=i=1∏n​2πσ2​1​exp(−2σ2(yi​−β0​−β1​xi​)2​),lnL=−2n​ln(2πσ2)−2σ21​J(β0​,β1​). The first term does not depend on (β0,β1)(\beta_0,\beta_1)(β0​,β1​) and 1/(2σ2)>01/(2\sigma^2)>01/(2σ2)>0, so maximising ln⁡L\ln LlnL ≡\equiv≡ minimising JJJ: (β^0,β^1)ML=(β^0,β^1)LS(\hat\beta_0,\hat\beta_1)_{ML}=(\hat\beta_0,\hat\beta_1)_{LS}(β^​0​,β^​1​)ML​=(β^​0​,β^​1​)LS​.

    MLE of σ2\sigma^2σ2 (slide 7)

    For every σ2\sigma^2σ2 the maximiser over (β0,β1)(\beta_0,\beta_1)(β0​,β1​) is still the LS fit. Plug it in and set ∂ln⁡L∂σ2=−n2σ2+J(β^0,β^1)2σ4=0\dfrac{\partial\ln L}{\partial\sigma^2}=-\dfrac{n}{2\sigma^2}+\dfrac{J(\hat\beta_0,\hat\beta_1)}{2\sigma^4}=0∂σ2∂lnL​=−2σ2n​+2σ4J(β^​0​,β^​1​)​=0: σ^ML2=J(β^0,β^1)n=1n∑i=1nei2.\hat\sigma^2_{ML}=\frac{J(\hat\beta_0,\hat\beta_1)}{n}=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n e_i^2 .σ^ML2​=nJ(β^​0​,β^​1​)​=n1​i=1∑n​ei2​. Like the sample variance with 1/n1/n1/n, this is biased; 1n−2∑iei2\frac{1}{n-2}\sum_i e_i^2n−21​∑i​ei2​ is unbiased (BT9.19).

    Another noise model, another loss (slide 8)

    Laplace noise fε(e)=12be−∣e∣/bf_\varepsilon(e)=\frac{1}{2b}e^{-|e|/b}fε​(e)=2b1​e−∣e∣/b gives ln⁡L=−nln⁡(2b)−1b∑i∣ei∣\ln L=-n\ln(2b)-\frac1b\sum_i|e_i|lnL=−nln(2b)−b1​∑i​∣ei​∣: the MLE minimises ∑i∣yi−β0−β1xi∣\sum_i|y_i-\beta_0-\beta_1x_i|∑i​∣yi​−β0​−β1​xi​∣ (least absolute deviations), which is robust to outliers, like the median versus the mean. The noise model decides the loss.

    Regression through the origin

    Model Yi=βxi+εiY_i=\beta x_i+\varepsilon_iYi​=βxi​+εi​: minimise J(β)=∑i(yi−βxi)2J(\beta)=\sum_i(y_i-\beta x_i)^2J(β)=∑i​(yi​−βxi​)2; J′(β)=−2∑ixi(yi−βxi)=0J'(\beta)=-2\sum_i x_i(y_i-\beta x_i)=0J′(β)=−2∑i​xi​(yi​−βxi​)=0 gives β^=∑ixiyi/∑ixi2\hat\beta=\sum_i x_iy_i/\sum_i x_i^2β^​=∑i​xi​yi​/∑i​xi2​ (a minimum since J′′=2∑xi2>0J''=2\sum x_i^2>0J′′=2∑xi2​>0). Only ∑ixiei=0\sum_i x_ie_i=0∑i​xi​ei​=0 holds.

    Comparing two fitted models

    With Gaussian noise of the same variance, the log likelihood of a fitted model is −n2ln⁡(2πσ2)−SSE/(2σ2)-\frac n2\ln(2\pi\sigma^2)-\text{SSE}/(2\sigma^2)−2n​ln(2πσ2)−SSE/(2σ2). With equal prior probabilities, the MAP rule picks the model with the larger likelihood, i.e. the smaller sum of squared residuals. A model that is linear in its parameters (e.g. β0+β1x2\beta_0+\beta_1x^2β0​+β1​x2) is fitted with the same formulas, with xi2x_i^2xi2​ in place of xix_ixi​.

    Watch out

    State why YiY_iYi​ is normal and why the YiY_iYi​ are independent (the xix_ixi​ are constants and the εi\varepsilon_iεi​ are independent) before writing the product likelihood. And argue that maximising ln⁡L\ln LlnL is minimising JJJ because the coefficient 1/(2σ2)1/(2\sigma^2)1/(2σ2) is positive.

    SQ26.1Regression through the origin: MLEs of β∗\beta^*β∗ and σ2\sigma^2σ2 2026 Surprise Quiz · Q1 · 10 marks★ Must-do

    Let Yi=β∗xi+εiY_i=\beta^*x_i+\varepsilon_iYi​=β∗xi​+εi​, i=1,…,ni=1,\dots,ni=1,…,n, where x1,…,xnx_1,\dots,x_nx1​,…,xn​ are known constants (not all zero) and ε1,…,εn\varepsilon_1,\dots,\varepsilon_nε1​,…,εn​ are i.i.d. N(0,σ2)\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2)N(0,σ2). Both β∗\beta^*β∗ and σ2\sigma^2σ2 are unknown. Given observations y1,…,yny_1,\dots,y_ny1​,…,yn​, derive the maximum likelihood estimates of β∗\beta^*β∗ and σ2\sigma^2σ2.

    Similar to: T26-14.6(a) (the same model, β\betaβ only).

    Solution · written for this guide, in the style of the course MLE keys (cf. ES23.A3)

    Distribution of the data

    The xix_ixi​ are constants and the εi\varepsilon_iεi​ are independent N(0,σ2)N(0,\sigma^2)N(0,σ2), so the YiY_iYi​ are independent with Yi∼N(β∗xi,σ2)Y_i\sim N(\beta^*x_i,\sigma^2)Yi​∼N(β∗xi​,σ2).

    Log-likelihood

    L(β,σ2)=∏i=1n12πσ2exp⁡ ⁣(−(yi−βxi)22σ2),ℓ(β,σ2)=−n2log⁡(2πσ2)−12σ2∑i=1n(yi−βxi)2.L(\beta,\sigma^2)=\prod_{i=1}^n\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}\exp\!\Big(-\frac{(y_i-\beta x_i)^2}{2\sigma^2}\Big),\qquad \ell(\beta,\sigma^2)=-\frac n2\log(2\pi\sigma^2)-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-\beta x_i)^2 .L(β,σ2)=i=1∏n​2πσ2​1​exp(−2σ2(yi​−βxi​)2​),ℓ(β,σ2)=−2n​log(2πσ2)−2σ21​i=1∑n​(yi​−βxi​)2.

    MLE of β∗\beta^*β∗

    For every fixed σ2\sigma^2σ2, β\betaβ appears only in −12σ2J(β)-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}J(\beta)−2σ21​J(β) with J(β)=∑i(yi−βxi)2J(\beta)=\sum_i(y_i-\beta x_i)^2J(β)=∑i​(yi​−βxi​)2, and 12σ2>0\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\gt02σ21​>0, so maximising ℓ\ellℓ over β\betaβ means minimising JJJ:

    ∂ℓ∂β=1σ2∑i=1nxi(yi−βxi)=0 ⟹ β^ML=∑i=1nxiyi∑i=1nxi2,\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial\beta}=\frac{1}{\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n x_i(y_i-\beta x_i)=0\ \Longrightarrow\ \hat\beta_{ML}=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n x_iy_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2},∂β∂ℓ​=σ21​i=1∑n​xi​(yi​−βxi​)=0 ⟹ β^​ML​=∑i=1n​xi2​∑i=1n​xi​yi​​,

    which is well defined since ∑xi2>0\sum x_i^2\gt0∑xi2​>0 (the xix_ixi​ are not all zero). It is a maximum: ∂2ℓ∂β2=−1σ2∑xi2<0\frac{\partial^2\ell}{\partial\beta^2}=-\frac{1}{\sigma^2}\sum x_i^2\lt0∂β2∂2ℓ​=−σ21​∑xi2​<0. The answer does not depend on σ2\sigma^2σ2.

    MLE of σ2\sigma^2σ2

    Substitute β^\hat\betaβ^​ and write v=σ2v=\sigma^2v=σ2, J0=J(β^)=∑i(yi−β^xi)2J_0=J(\hat\beta)=\sum_i(y_i-\hat\beta x_i)^2J0​=J(β^​)=∑i​(yi​−β^​xi​)2:

    ∂ℓ∂v=−n2v+J02v2=0 ⟹ σ^ML2=J0n=1n∑i=1n(yi−β^MLxi)2.\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial v}=-\frac{n}{2v}+\frac{J_0}{2v^2}=0\ \Longrightarrow\ \hat\sigma^2_{ML}=\frac{J_0}{n}=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\big(y_i-\hat\beta_{ML}x_i\big)^2 .∂v∂ℓ​=−2vn​+2v2J0​​=0 ⟹ σ^ML2​=nJ0​​=n1​i=1∑n​(yi​−β^​ML​xi​)2.

    Maximum: ∂ℓ∂v=J0−nv2v2\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial v}=\frac{J_0-nv}{2v^2}∂v∂ℓ​=2v2J0​−nv​ is positive for v<J0/nv\lt J_0/nv<J0​/n and negative after. Jointly, ℓ(β,v)≤ℓ(β^,v)≤ℓ(β^,σ^2)\ell(\beta,v)\le\ell(\hat\beta,v)\le\ell(\hat\beta,\hat\sigma^2)ℓ(β,v)≤ℓ(β^​,v)≤ℓ(β^​,σ^2) for all (β,v)(\beta,v)(β,v), so (β^,σ^2)(\hat\beta,\hat\sigma^2)(β^​,σ^2) is the joint maximiser (assuming J0>0J_0\gt0J0​>0, which holds with probability 1 when n≥2n\ge2n≥2).

    Extra (not asked): E[σ^ML2]=n−1nσ2E[\hat\sigma^2_{ML}]=\frac{n-1}{n}\sigma^2E[σ^ML2​]=nn−1​σ2 (one parameter fitted), so it is biased; 1n−1J0\frac{1}{n-1}J_0n−11​J0​ is unbiased.

    What the grader checks (no key; inferred from the course MLE keys)
    • YiY_iYi​ independent N(β∗xi,σ2)N(\beta^*x_i,\sigma^2)N(β∗xi​,σ2), with the reason.
    • Likelihood and log-likelihood in both parameters.
    • ∂ℓ/∂β=0⇒β^=∑xiyi/∑xi2\partial\ell/\partial\beta=0\Rightarrow\hat\beta=\sum x_iy_i/\sum x_i^2∂ℓ/∂β=0⇒β^​=∑xi​yi​/∑xi2​ (uses "not all zero").
    • ∂ℓ/∂σ2=0\partial\ell/\partial\sigma^2=0∂ℓ/∂σ2=0 with β^\hat\betaβ^​ plugged in ⇒σ^2=1n∑(yi−β^xi)2\Rightarrow\hat\sigma^2=\frac1n\sum(y_i-\hat\beta x_i)^2⇒σ^2=n1​∑(yi​−β^​xi​)2; a maximum check.
    Answer

    β^ML=∑ixiyi∑ixi2\hat\beta_{ML}=\dfrac{\sum_i x_iy_i}{\sum_i x_i^2}β^​ML​=∑i​xi2​∑i​xi​yi​​, σ^ML2=1n∑i(yi−β^MLxi)2\hat\sigma^2_{ML}=\dfrac1n\sum_i\big(y_i-\hat\beta_{ML}x_i\big)^2σ^ML2​=n1​∑i​(yi​−β^​ML​xi​)2.

    Tutorials and homeworks

    T26-14.6Regression through the origin: MLE and residuals 2026 Tut 14 Q6
    (Regression through the origin) Suppose the model is Yi=βxi+εiY_i=\beta x_i+\varepsilon_iYi​=βxi​+εi​ for i=1,…,ni=1,\dots,ni=1,…,n (no intercept), where εi∼N(0,σ2)\varepsilon_i\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2)εi​∼N(0,σ2) are i.i.d. and the xix_ixi​ are fixed constants (not all zero).
    1. Derive the maximum likelihood estimate β^\hat\betaβ^​ by minimising ∑i=1n(yi−βxi)2\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-\beta x_i)^2∑i=1n​(yi​−βxi​)2.
    2. For the data (1,2),(2,3),(3,7)(1,2),(2,3),(3,7)(1,2),(2,3),(3,7), compute β^\hat\betaβ^​ and verify whether the residuals sum to zero.

    [The sheet has no part (b).]

    Solution · written for this guide

    (a) The MLE

    The xix_ixi​ are constants and εi∼N(0,σ2)\varepsilon_i\sim N(0,\sigma^2)εi​∼N(0,σ2) are independent, so the Yi=βxi+εiY_i=\beta x_i+\varepsilon_iYi​=βxi​+εi​ are independent with Yi∼N(βxi,σ2)Y_i\sim N(\beta x_i,\sigma^2)Yi​∼N(βxi​,σ2). The likelihood is

    L(β)=∏i=1n12πσ2e−(yi−βxi)2/(2σ2),ln⁡L(β)=−n2ln⁡(2πσ2)−12σ2∑i=1n(yi−βxi)2.L(\beta)=\prod_{i=1}^n\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}e^{-(y_i-\beta x_i)^2/(2\sigma^2)},\qquad \ln L(\beta)=-\frac n2\ln(2\pi\sigma^2)-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-\beta x_i)^2 .L(β)=i=1∏n​2πσ2​1​e−(yi​−βxi​)2/(2σ2),lnL(β)=−2n​ln(2πσ2)−2σ21​i=1∑n​(yi​−βxi​)2.

    The first term does not involve β\betaβ and 1/(2σ2)>01/(2\sigma^2)>01/(2σ2)>0, so maximising ln⁡L\ln LlnL is the same as minimising J(β)=∑i(yi−βxi)2J(\beta)=\sum_i(y_i-\beta x_i)^2J(β)=∑i​(yi​−βxi​)2.

    J′(β)=−2∑ixi(yi−βxi)=0 ⟹ ∑ixiyi=β∑ixi2 ⟹ β^=∑i=1nxiyi∑i=1nxi2.J'(\beta)=-2\sum_i x_i(y_i-\beta x_i)=0\ \Longrightarrow\ \sum_i x_iy_i=\beta\sum_i x_i^2\ \Longrightarrow\ \hat\beta=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n x_iy_i}{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2}.J′(β)=−2i∑​xi​(yi​−βxi​)=0 ⟹ i∑​xi​yi​=βi∑​xi2​ ⟹ β^​=∑i=1n​xi2​∑i=1n​xi​yi​​.

    This is a minimum: J′′(β)=2∑ixi2>0J''(\beta)=2\sum_i x_i^2>0J′′(β)=2∑i​xi2​>0 because the xix_ixi​ are not all zero (so JJJ is a strictly convex quadratic).

    (c) The data

    ∑xiyi=1⋅2+2⋅3+3⋅7=29,∑xi2=1+4+9=14,β^=2914≈2.071.\sum x_iy_i=1\cdot2+2\cdot3+3\cdot7=29,\qquad \sum x_i^2=1+4+9=14,\qquad \hat\beta=\frac{29}{14}\approx2.071 .∑xi​yi​=1⋅2+2⋅3+3⋅7=29,∑xi2​=1+4+9=14,β^​=1429​≈2.071.

    Residuals ei=yi−β^xie_i=y_i-\hat\beta x_iei​=yi​−β^​xi​:

    PCS8.5.5.5Maximum likelihood gives least squares PC §8.5.5 Solved Problem 5
    (The Method of Maximum Likelihood) Consider the model Yi=β0+β1xi+ϵiY_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i+\epsilon_iYi​=β0​+β1​xi​+ϵi​, where the ϵi\epsilon_iϵi​'s are independent N(0,σ2)N(0,\sigma^2)N(0,σ2) random variables. Our goal is to estimate β0\beta_0β0​ and β1\beta_1β1​. We have the observed data pairs (x1,y1),…,(xn,yn)(x_1,y_1),\dots,(x_n,y_n)(x1​,y1​),…,(xn​,yn​).
    1. Argue that, for given values of β0\beta_0β0​, β1\beta_1β1​, and xix_ixi​, YiY_iYi​ is a normal random variable with mean β0+β1xi\beta_0+\beta_1x_iβ0​+β1​xi​ and variance σ2\sigma^2σ2. Moreover, show that the YiY_iYi​'s are independent.
    2. Find the likelihood function L(y1,…,yn;β0,β1)=fY1⋯Yn(y1,…,yn;β0,β1)L(y_1,\dots,y_n;\beta_0,\beta_1)=f_{Y_1\cdots Y_n}(y_1,\dots,y_n;\beta_0,\beta_1)L(y1​,…,yn​;β0​,β1​)=fY1​⋯Yn​​(y1​,…,yn​;β0​,β1​).
    3. Show that the maximum likelihood estimates of β0\beta_0β0​ and β1\beta_1β1​ are the same as the ones we obtained using the least squares method.
    Solution · follows ProbabilityCourse's solution

    (a)

    For given β0,β1,xi\beta_0,\beta_1,x_iβ0​,β1​,xi​, ci=β0+β1xic_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_ici​=β0​+β1​xi​ is a constant, so Yi=ci+ϵiY_i=c_i+\epsilon_iYi​=ci​+ϵi​ is a shifted N(0,σ2)N(0,\sigma^2)N(0,σ2): Yi∼N(β0+β1xi,σ2)Y_i\sim N(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i,\sigma^2)Yi​∼N(β0​+β1​xi​,σ2). Each YiY_iYi​ is a function of ϵi\epsilon_iϵi​ alone, and functions of independent random variables are independent, so the YiY_iYi​ are independent.

    (b)

    L=∏i=1nfYi(yi)=1(2πσ2)n/2exp⁡{−12σ2∑i=1n(yi−β0−β1xi)2}.L=\prod_{i=1}^n f_{Y_i}(y_i)=\frac{1}{(2\pi\sigma^2)^{n/2}}\exp\Big\{-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-\beta_0-\beta_1x_i)^2\Big\}.L=i=1∏n​fYi​​(yi​)=(2πσ2)n/21​exp{−2σ21​i=1∑n​(yi​−β0​−β1​xi​)2}.

    (c)

    e−ue^{-u}e−u is decreasing in uuu and the prefactor does not depend on (β0,β1)(\beta_0,\beta_1)(β0​,β1​), so LLL is maximised exactly when J(β0,β1)=∑i(yi−β0−β1xi)2J(\beta_0,\beta_1)=\sum_i(y_i-\beta_0-\beta_1x_i)^2J(β0​,β1​)=∑i​(yi​−β0​−β1​xi​)2 is minimised. That is the least-squares problem, whose solution (normal equations) is β^1=Sxy/Sxx\hat\beta_1=S_{xy}/S_{xx}β^​1​=Sxy​/Sxx​, β^0=yˉ−β^1xˉ\hat\beta_0=\bar y-\hat\beta_1\bar xβ^​0​=yˉ​−β^​1​xˉ.

    Answer

    (β^0,β^1)ML=arg⁡min⁡J=(yˉ−β^1xˉ, Sxy/Sxx)(\hat\beta_0,\hat\beta_1)_{ML}=\arg\min J=(\bar y-\hat\beta_1\bar x,\ S_{xy}/S_{xx})(β^​0​,β^​1​)ML​=argminJ=(yˉ​−β^​1​xˉ, Sxy​/Sxx​), the least-squares estimates.

    3  Sampling properties: bias, variance, MSE · slides 7, 9

    Theory recap

    Condition on the xix_ixi​: they are constants, only the YiY_iYi​ (through the noise) are random. Repeating the experiment gives new noise and a new fitted line, so β^0,β^1\hat\beta_0,\hat\beta_1β^​0​,β^​1​ are random variables (slide 9).

    The key trick: linear forms

    Because ∑i(xi−xˉ)=0\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)=0∑i​(xi​−xˉ)=0, SxY=∑i(xi−xˉ)(Yi−Yˉ)=∑i(xi−xˉ)YiS_{xY}=\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)(Y_i-\bar Y)=\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)Y_iSxY​=∑i​(xi​−xˉ)(Yi​−Yˉ)=∑i​(xi​−xˉ)Yi​, so β^1=∑i=1nkiYi,ki=xi−xˉSxx;β^0=Yˉ−β^1xˉ=∑i=1nciYi,ci=1n−xˉ(xi−xˉ)Sxx.\hat\beta_1=\sum_{i=1}^n k_iY_i,\quad k_i=\frac{x_i-\bar x}{S_{xx}};\qquad \hat\beta_0=\bar Y-\hat\beta_1\bar x=\sum_{i=1}^n c_iY_i,\quad c_i=\frac1n-\frac{\bar x(x_i-\bar x)}{S_{xx}} .β^​1​=i=1∑n​ki​Yi​,ki​=Sxx​xi​−xˉ​;β^​0​=Yˉ−β^​1​xˉ=i=1∑n​ci​Yi​,ci​=n1​−Sxx​xˉ(xi​−xˉ)​. Facts about the weights: ∑ki=0\sum k_i=0∑ki​=0, ∑kixi=1\sum k_ix_i=1∑ki​xi​=1, ∑ki2=1/Sxx\sum k_i^2=1/S_{xx}∑ki2​=1/Sxx​. With Gaussian noise, a linear combination of independent normals is normal, so β^0,β^1\hat\beta_0,\hat\beta_1β^​0​,β^​1​ are normal.

    Mean, variance, MSE (slide 9) E[β^1]=β1,E[β^0]=β0,E[\hat\beta_1]=\beta_1,\qquad E[\hat\beta_0]=\beta_0,E[β^​1​]=β1​,E[β^​0​]=β0​, Var⁡(β^1)=σ2Sxx,Var⁡(β^0)=σ2(1n+xˉ2Sxx)=σ2∑ixi2nSxx,\operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta_1)=\frac{\sigma^2}{S_{xx}},\qquad \operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta_0)=\sigma^2\Big(\frac1n+\frac{\bar x^2}{S_{xx}}\Big)=\frac{\sigma^2\sum_i x_i^2}{nS_{xx}},Var(β^​1​)=Sxx​σ2​,Var(β^​0​)=σ2(n1​+Sxx​xˉ2​)=nSxx​σ2∑i​xi2​​, Cov⁡(β^1,Yi)=xi−xˉSxxσ2,Cov⁡(β^1,Yˉ)=0,Cov⁡(β^0,β^1)=−xˉσ2Sxx.\operatorname{Cov}(\hat\beta_1,Y_i)=\frac{x_i-\bar x}{S_{xx}}\sigma^2,\quad \operatorname{Cov}(\hat\beta_1,\bar Y)=0,\quad \operatorname{Cov}(\hat\beta_0,\hat\beta_1)=-\frac{\bar x\sigma^2}{S_{xx}} .Cov(β^​1​,Yi​)=Sxx​xi​−xˉ​σ2,Cov(β^​1​,Yˉ)=0,Cov(β^​0​,β^​1​)=−Sxx​xˉσ2​.

    Unbiased, so MSE=Var⁡+bias2=Var⁡\text{MSE}=\operatorname{Var}+\text{bias}^2=\operatorname{Var}MSE=Var+bias2=Var. Unbiasedness needs only E[εi]=0E[\varepsilon_i]=0E[εi​]=0; the variances need only uncorrelated noise with variance σ2\sigma^2σ2; normality needs Gaussian noise.

    Estimating σ2\sigma^2σ2 (slide 7) E[∑iei2]=(n−2)σ2,sos2=1n−2∑iei2 is unbiased and σ^ML2=1n∑ei2 has bias −2σ2n.E\Big[\sum_i e_i^2\Big]=(n-2)\sigma^2,\qquad\text{so}\quad s^2=\frac{1}{n-2}\sum_i e_i^2\ \text{is unbiased and}\ \hat\sigma^2_{ML}=\frac1n\sum e_i^2\ \text{has bias}\ -\frac{2\sigma^2}{n}.E[i∑​ei2​]=(n−2)σ2,sos2=n−21​i∑​ei2​ is unbiased and σ^ML2​=n1​∑ei2​ has bias −n2σ2​.

    Two parameters were fitted, so two "degrees of freedom" are used up (the two normal equations constrain the residuals).

    Consistency

    Unbiased with variance →0\to0→0 gives MSE →0\to0→0, hence consistency (Chebyshev). Here Var⁡(β^1)=σ2/Sxx→0\operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta_1)=\sigma^2/S_{xx}\to0Var(β^​1​)=σ2/Sxx​→0 when Sxx→∞S_{xx}\to\inftySxx​→∞, and Var⁡(β^0)=σ2/n+xˉ2σ2/Sxx→0\operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta_0)=\sigma^2/n+\bar x^2\sigma^2/S_{xx}\to0Var(β^​0​)=σ2/n+xˉ2σ2/Sxx​→0 if also xˉ2\bar x^2xˉ2 stays bounded.

    Watch out

    Var⁡(Yˉ−β^1xˉ)\operatorname{Var}(\bar Y-\hat\beta_1\bar x)Var(Yˉ−β^​1​xˉ) is not Var⁡Yˉ+xˉ2Var⁡β^1\operatorname{Var}\bar Y+\bar x^2\operatorname{Var}\hat\beta_1VarYˉ+xˉ2Varβ^​1​ until you have shown Cov⁡(Yˉ,β^1)=0\operatorname{Cov}(\bar Y,\hat\beta_1)=0Cov(Yˉ,β^​1​)=0. Say it. And Var⁡(∑kiYi)=∑ki2Var⁡Yi\operatorname{Var}(\sum k_iY_i)=\sum k_i^2\operatorname{Var}Y_iVar(∑ki​Yi​)=∑ki2​VarYi​ uses independence of the YiY_iYi​.

    H26-12.1Bias, variance and MSE of β^1\hat\beta_1β^​1​ and β^0\hat\beta_0β^​0​ 2026 HW 12 Q1
    Consider the simple linear regression model Yi=β0+β1xi+ϵiY_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i+\epsilon_iYi​=β0​+β1​xi​+ϵi​ for i=1,2,…,ni=1,2,\dots,ni=1,2,…,n, where the ϵi\epsilon_iϵi​'s are independent N(0,σ2)\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2)N(0,σ2) random variables. The least-squares estimators are: β^1=SxySxx,β^0=Yˉ−β^1xˉ\hat\beta_1=\frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}},\qquad \hat\beta_0=\bar Y-\hat\beta_1\bar xβ^​1​=Sxx​Sxy​​,β^​0​=Yˉ−β^​1​xˉ where Sxx=∑i=1n(xi−xˉ)2S_{xx}=\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)^2Sxx​=∑i=1n​(xi​−xˉ)2, Sxy=∑i=1n(xi−xˉ)(Yi−Yˉ)S_{xy}=\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)(Y_i-\bar Y)Sxy​=∑i=1n​(xi​−xˉ)(Yi​−Yˉ).
    1. Find the bias, variance, and Mean Squared Error (MSE) of the slope estimator β^1\hat\beta_1β^​1​.
    2. Find the bias, variance, and Mean Squared Error (MSE) of the intercept estimator β^0\hat\beta_0β^​0​.

    Overlaps H25-11.6 and H25-11.7 (which ask for the same facts as "show that"); also PC §8.6 Problems 23–24.

    Solution · written for this guide (in the style of the 2025 course solutions)

    Treat x1,…,xnx_1,\dots,x_nx1​,…,xn​ as constants. Then YiY_iYi​ are independent with E[Yi]=β0+β1xiE[Y_i]=\beta_0+\beta_1x_iE[Yi​]=β0​+β1​xi​ and Var⁡(Yi)=σ2\operatorname{Var}(Y_i)=\sigma^2Var(Yi​)=σ2.

    (a) The slope

    Linear form. Since ∑i(xi−xˉ)=0\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)=0∑i​(xi​−xˉ)=0, Sxy=∑i(xi−xˉ)Yi−Yˉ∑i(xi−xˉ)=∑i(xi−xˉ)YiS_{xy}=\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)Y_i-\bar Y\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)=\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)Y_iSxy​=∑i​(xi​−xˉ)Yi​−Yˉ∑i​(xi​−xˉ)=∑i​(xi​−xˉ)Yi​, so

    β^1=∑i=1nkiYi,ki=xi−xˉSxx (constants).\hat\beta_1=\sum_{i=1}^n k_iY_i,\qquad k_i=\frac{x_i-\bar x}{S_{xx}}\ \text{(constants)} .β^​1​=i=1∑n​ki​Yi​,ki​=Sxx​xi​−xˉ​ (constants).

    Mean (linearity of expectation):

    E[β^1]=∑iki(β0+β1xi)=β0∑i(xi−xˉ)+β1∑i(xi−xˉ)xiSxx=0+β1SxxSxx=β1,E[\hat\beta_1]=\sum_i k_i(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i)=\frac{\beta_0\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)+\beta_1\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)x_i}{S_{xx}}=\frac{0+\beta_1S_{xx}}{S_{xx}}=\beta_1,E[β^​1​]=i∑​ki​(β0​+β1​xi​)=Sxx​β0​∑i​(xi​−xˉ)+β1​∑i​(xi​−xˉ)xi​​=Sxx​0+β1​Sxx​​=β1​,

    using ∑i(xi−xˉ)xi=∑i(xi−xˉ)(xi−xˉ)=Sxx\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)x_i=\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)(x_i-\bar x)=S_{xx}∑i​(xi​−xˉ)xi​=∑i​(xi​−xˉ)(xi​−xˉ)=Sxx​. So Bias⁡(β^1)=0\operatorname{Bias}(\hat\beta_1)=0Bias(β^​1​)=0.

    Variance (the YiY_iYi​ are independent):

    Var⁡(β^1)=∑iki2Var⁡(Yi)=σ2Sxx2∑i(xi−xˉ)2=σ2Sxx.\operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta_1)=\sum_i k_i^2\operatorname{Var}(Y_i)=\frac{\sigma^2}{S_{xx}^2}\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2=\frac{\sigma^2}{S_{xx}} .Var(β^​1​)=i∑​ki2​Var(Yi​)=Sxx2​σ2​i∑​(xi​−xˉ)2=Sxx​σ2​.

    MSE =Var⁡+Bias⁡2=σ2/Sxx=\operatorname{Var}+\operatorname{Bias}^2=\sigma^2/S_{xx}=Var+Bias2=σ2/Sxx​.

    (b) The intercept

    Mean. E[Yˉ]=1n∑i(β0+β1xi)=β0+β1xˉE[\bar Y]=\frac1n\sum_i(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i)=\beta_0+\beta_1\bar xE[Yˉ]=n1​∑i​(β0​+β1​xi​)=β0​+β1​xˉ, so E[β^0]=E[Yˉ]−xˉE[β^1]=β0+β1xˉ−β1xˉ=β0E[\hat\beta_0]=E[\bar Y]-\bar xE[\hat\beta_1]=\beta_0+\beta_1\bar x-\beta_1\bar x=\beta_0E[β^​0​]=E[Yˉ]−xˉE[β^​1​]=β0​+β1​xˉ−β1​xˉ=β0​. Bias =0=0=0.

    A covariance we need. By bilinearity and independence (Cov⁡(Yi,Yj)=0\operatorname{Cov}(Y_i,Y_j)=0Cov(Yi​,Yj​)=0 for i≠ji\neq ji=j),

    Cov⁡(Yˉ,β^1)=Cov⁡(1n∑jYj,∑ikiYi)=1n∑ikiσ2=σ2nSxx∑i(xi−xˉ)=0.\operatorname{Cov}(\bar Y,\hat\beta_1)=\operatorname{Cov}\Big(\frac1n\sum_jY_j,\sum_ik_iY_i\Big)=\frac1n\sum_ik_i\sigma^2=\frac{\sigma^2}{nS_{xx}}\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)=0 .Cov(Yˉ,β^​1​)=Cov(n1​j∑​Yj​,i∑​ki​Yi​)=n1​i∑​ki​σ2=nSxx​σ2​i∑​(xi​−xˉ)=0.

    Variance. xˉ\bar xxˉ is a constant, so

    Var⁡(β^0)=Var⁡(Yˉ)+xˉ2Var⁡(β^1)−2xˉCov⁡(Yˉ,β^1)=σ2n+xˉ2σ2Sxx.\operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta_0)=\operatorname{Var}(\bar Y)+\bar x^2\operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta_1)-2\bar x\operatorname{Cov}(\bar Y,\hat\beta_1)=\frac{\sigma^2}{n}+\frac{\bar x^2\sigma^2}{S_{xx}} .Var(β^​0​)=Var(Yˉ)+xˉ2Var(β^​1​)−2xˉCov(Yˉ,β^​1​)=nσ2​+Sxx​xˉ2σ2​.

    Using Sxx+nxˉ2=∑ixi2S_{xx}+n\bar x^2=\sum_ix_i^2Sxx​+nxˉ2=∑i​xi2​: Var⁡(β^0)=σ2Sxx+nxˉ2nSxx=σ2∑ixi2nSxx\operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta_0)=\sigma^2\dfrac{S_{xx}+n\bar x^2}{nS_{xx}}=\dfrac{\sigma^2\sum_ix_i^2}{nS_{xx}}Var(β^​0​)=σ2nSxx​Sxx​+nxˉ2​=nSxx​σ2∑i​xi2​​.

    MSE =Var⁡(β^0)=\operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta_0)=Var(β^​0​) since the bias is 0.

    Answer

    (a) Bias⁡(β^1)=0, Var⁡(β^1)=MSE⁡(β^1)=σ2/Sxx\operatorname{Bias}(\hat\beta_1)=0,\ \operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta_1)=\operatorname{MSE}(\hat\beta_1)=\sigma^2/S_{xx}Bias(β^​1​)=0, Var(β^​1​)=MSE(β^​1​)=σ2/Sxx​.
    (b) Bias⁡(β^0)=0, Var⁡(β^0)=MSE⁡(β^0)=σ2(1n+xˉ2Sxx)=σ2∑xi2nSxx\operatorname{Bias}(\hat\beta_0)=0,\ \operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta_0)=\operatorname{MSE}(\hat\beta_0)=\sigma^2\big(\tfrac1n+\tfrac{\bar x^2}{S_{xx}}\big)=\tfrac{\sigma^2\sum x_i^2}{nS_{xx}}Bias(β^​0​)=0, Var(β^​0​)=MSE(β^​0​)=σ2(n1​+Sxx​xˉ2​)=nSxx​σ2∑xi2​​.

    H25-11.6β^1\hat\beta_1β^​1​ is normal, unbiased, with variance σ2/Sxx\sigma^2/S_{xx}σ2/Sxx​ 2025 HW 11 Q6
    Consider the simple linear regression model Yi=β0+β1xi+ϵiY_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i+\epsilon_iYi​=β0​+β1​xi​+ϵi​, where ϵi\epsilon_iϵi​'s are independent N(0,σ2)N(0,\sigma^2)N(0,σ2) random variables. The estimators are: β^1=SxySxx,β^0=Yˉ−β^1xˉ\hat\beta_1=\frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}},\qquad \hat\beta_0=\bar Y-\hat\beta_1\bar xβ^​1​=Sxx​Sxy​​,β^​0​=Yˉ−β^​1​xˉ where Sxx=∑i=1n(xi−xˉ)2S_{xx}=\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)^2Sxx​=∑i=1n​(xi​−xˉ)2, Sxy=∑i=1n(xi−xˉ)(Yi−Yˉ)S_{xy}=\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)(Y_i-\bar Y)Sxy​=∑i=1n​(xi​−xˉ)(Yi​−Yˉ).
    1. Show that β^1\hat\beta_1β^​1​ is a normal random variable.
    2. Show that E[β^1]=β1E[\hat\beta_1]=\beta_1E[β^​1​]=β1​.
    3. Show that Var⁡(β^1)=σ2Sxx\operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta_1)=\frac{\sigma^2}{S_{xx}}Var(β^​1​)=Sxx​σ2​.

    Same as PC §8.6 Problem 23 (identical wording). Overlaps H26-12.1(a).

    Solution · follows the 2025 course solutions

    (a) Normality

    Since ∑(xi−xˉ)=0\sum(x_i-\bar x)=0∑(xi​−xˉ)=0,

    Sxy=∑(xi−xˉ)(Yi−Yˉ)=∑(xi−xˉ)Yi−Yˉ∑(xi−xˉ)=∑i=1n(xi−xˉ)Yi,β^1=∑i=1n(xi−xˉSxx)Yi=∑i=1nkiYi.S_{xy}=\sum(x_i-\bar x)(Y_i-\bar Y)=\sum(x_i-\bar x)Y_i-\bar Y\sum(x_i-\bar x)=\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)Y_i, \qquad \hat\beta_1=\sum_{i=1}^n\Big(\frac{x_i-\bar x}{S_{xx}}\Big)Y_i=\sum_{i=1}^n k_iY_i .Sxy​=∑(xi​−xˉ)(Yi​−Yˉ)=∑(xi​−xˉ)Yi​−Yˉ∑(xi​−xˉ)=i=1∑n​(xi​−xˉ)Yi​,β^​1​=i=1∑n​(Sxx​xi​−xˉ​)Yi​=i=1∑n​ki​Yi​.

    ki=(xi−xˉ)/Sxxk_i=(x_i-\bar x)/S_{xx}ki​=(xi​−xˉ)/Sxx​ is a constant because xi,xˉ,Sxxx_i,\bar x,S_{xx}xi​,xˉ,Sxx​ are fixed. Each Yi=β0+β1xi+ϵiY_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i+\epsilon_iYi​=β0​+β1​xi​+ϵi​ is normal and the YiY_iYi​ are independent; a linear combination of independent normal random variables is normal, so β^1\hat\beta_1β^​1​ is normal.

    (b) Mean

    E[β^1]=∑kiE[Yi]=∑i=1nxi−xˉSxx(β0+β1xi)=1Sxx[β0∑(xi−xˉ)+β1∑(xi−xˉ)xi].E[\hat\beta_1]=\sum k_iE[Y_i]=\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{x_i-\bar x}{S_{xx}}(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i)=\frac{1}{S_{xx}}\Big[\beta_0\sum(x_i-\bar x)+\beta_1\sum(x_i-\bar x)x_i\Big] .E[β^​1​]=∑ki​E[Yi​]=i=1∑n​Sxx​xi​−xˉ​(β0​+β1​xi​)=Sxx​1​[β0​∑(xi​−xˉ)+β1​∑(xi​−xˉ)xi​].

    The first sum is 0; the second is β1∑(xi−xˉ)xi=β1∑(xi−xˉ)2=β1Sxx\beta_1\sum(x_i-\bar x)x_i=\beta_1\sum(x_i-\bar x)^2=\beta_1S_{xx}β1​∑(xi​−xˉ)xi​=β1​∑(xi​−xˉ)2=β1​Sxx​. So E[β^1]=1Sxx[0+β1Sxx]=β1E[\hat\beta_1]=\frac{1}{S_{xx}}[0+\beta_1S_{xx}]=\beta_1E[β^​1​]=Sxx​1​[0+β1​Sxx​]=β1​.

    (c) Variance

    The YiY_iYi​ are independent, so

    Var⁡(β^1)=∑i=1nki2Var⁡(Yi)=∑i=1n(xi−xˉSxx)2σ2=σ2Sxx2∑(xi−xˉ)2=σ2Sxx.\operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta_1)=\sum_{i=1}^nk_i^2\operatorname{Var}(Y_i)=\sum_{i=1}^n\Big(\frac{x_i-\bar x}{S_{xx}}\Big)^2\sigma^2=\frac{\sigma^2}{S_{xx}^2}\sum(x_i-\bar x)^2=\frac{\sigma^2}{S_{xx}} .Var(β^​1​)=i=1∑n​ki2​Var(Yi​)=i=1∑n​(Sxx​xi​−xˉ​)2σ2=Sxx2​σ2​∑(xi​−xˉ)2=Sxx​σ2​.
    Answer

    β^1=∑kiYi∼N(β1, σ2/Sxx)\hat\beta_1=\sum k_iY_i\sim N\big(\beta_1,\ \sigma^2/S_{xx}\big)β^​1​=∑ki​Yi​∼N(β1​, σ2/Sxx​).

    H25-11.7β^0\hat\beta_0β^​0​: normal, unbiased, covariances, variance 2025 HW 11 Q7
    Again consider the simple linear regression model from Problem 1 [the model of H25-11.6].
    1. Show that β^0\hat\beta_0β^​0​ is a normal random variable.
    2. Show that E[β^0]=β0E[\hat\beta_0]=\beta_0E[β^​0​]=β0​.
    3. Show that Cov⁡(β^1,Yi)=xi−xˉSxxσ2\operatorname{Cov}(\hat\beta_1,Y_i)=\frac{x_i-\bar x}{S_{xx}}\sigma^2Cov(β^​1​,Yi​)=Sxx​xi​−xˉ​σ2.
    4. Show that Cov⁡(β^1,Yˉ)=0\operatorname{Cov}(\hat\beta_1,\bar Y)=0Cov(β^​1​,Yˉ)=0.
    5. Show that Var⁡(β^0)=∑i=1nxi2nSxxσ2\operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta_0)=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^nx_i^2}{nS_{xx}}\sigma^2Var(β^​0​)=nSxx​∑i=1n​xi2​​σ2.

    Same as PC §8.6 Problem 24 (identical wording). Overlaps H26-12.1(b).

    Solution · follows the 2025 course solutions

    (a) Normality

    With ki=(xi−xˉ)/Sxxk_i=(x_i-\bar x)/S_{xx}ki​=(xi​−xˉ)/Sxx​ from H25-11.6,

    β^0=1n∑Yi−xˉ∑kiYi=∑i=1n(1n−xˉ(xi−xˉ)Sxx)Yi=∑i=1nciYi.\hat\beta_0=\frac1n\sum Y_i-\bar x\sum k_iY_i=\sum_{i=1}^n\Big(\frac1n-\frac{\bar x(x_i-\bar x)}{S_{xx}}\Big)Y_i=\sum_{i=1}^nc_iY_i .β^​0​=n1​∑Yi​−xˉ∑ki​Yi​=i=1∑n​(n1​−Sxx​xˉ(xi​−xˉ)​)Yi​=i=1∑n​ci​Yi​.

    The cic_ici​ are constants, so β^0\hat\beta_0β^​0​ is a linear combination of independent normal random variables, hence normal.

    (b) Mean

    E[Yˉ]=1n∑(β0+β1xi)=β0+β1xˉ,E[β^0]=E[Yˉ]−xˉE[β^1]=(β0+β1xˉ)−β1xˉ=β0.E[\bar Y]=\frac1n\sum(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i)=\beta_0+\beta_1\bar x,\qquad E[\hat\beta_0]=E[\bar Y]-\bar xE[\hat\beta_1]=(\beta_0+\beta_1\bar x)-\beta_1\bar x=\beta_0 .E[Yˉ]=n1​∑(β0​+β1​xi​)=β0​+β1​xˉ,E[β^​0​]=E[Yˉ]−xˉE[β^​1​]=(β0​+β1​xˉ)−β1​xˉ=β0​.

    (c) Cov⁡(β^1,Yi)\operatorname{Cov}(\hat\beta_1,Y_i)Cov(β^​1​,Yi​)

    Cov⁡(β^1,Yi)=Cov⁡(∑jkjYj, Yi)=∑jkjCov⁡(Yj,Yi)=kiVar⁡(Yi)=xi−xˉSxxσ2,\operatorname{Cov}(\hat\beta_1,Y_i)=\operatorname{Cov}\Big(\sum_jk_jY_j,\ Y_i\Big)=\sum_jk_j\operatorname{Cov}(Y_j,Y_i)=k_i\operatorname{Var}(Y_i)=\frac{x_i-\bar x}{S_{xx}}\sigma^2,Cov(β^​1​,Yi​)=Cov(j∑​kj​Yj​, Yi​)=j∑​kj​Cov(Yj​,Yi​)=ki​Var(Yi​)=Sxx​xi​−xˉ​σ2,

    since Cov⁡(Yj,Yi)=0\operatorname{Cov}(Y_j,Y_i)=0Cov(Yj​,Yi​)=0 for j≠ij\neq ij=i (independence) and only the j=ij=ij=i term survives.

    (d) Cov⁡(β^1,Yˉ)\operatorname{Cov}(\hat\beta_1,\bar Y)Cov(β^​1​,Yˉ)

    Cov⁡(β^1,Yˉ)=1n∑i=1nCov⁡(β^1,Yi)=σ2nSxx∑i=1n(xi−xˉ)=0.\operatorname{Cov}(\hat\beta_1,\bar Y)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\operatorname{Cov}(\hat\beta_1,Y_i)=\frac{\sigma^2}{nS_{xx}}\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)=0 .Cov(β^​1​,Yˉ)=n1​i=1∑n​Cov(β^​1​,Yi​)=nSxx​σ2​i=1∑n​(xi​−xˉ)=0.

    (e) Var⁡(β^0)\operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta_0)Var(β^​0​)

    Var⁡(β^0)=Var⁡(Yˉ)+xˉ2Var⁡(β^1)−2xˉCov⁡(Yˉ,β^1)=Var⁡(Yˉ)+xˉ2Var⁡(β^1)by (d).\operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta_0)=\operatorname{Var}(\bar Y)+\bar x^2\operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta_1)-2\bar x\operatorname{Cov}(\bar Y,\hat\beta_1)=\operatorname{Var}(\bar Y)+\bar x^2\operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta_1)\quad\text{by (d)} .Var(β^​0​)=Var(Yˉ)+xˉ2Var(β^​1​)−2xˉCov(Yˉ,β^​1​)=Var(Yˉ)+xˉ2Var(β^​1​)by (d).

    Var⁡(Yˉ)=1n2∑Var⁡(Yi)=σ2n\operatorname{Var}(\bar Y)=\frac{1}{n^2}\sum\operatorname{Var}(Y_i)=\frac{\sigma^2}{n}Var(Yˉ)=n21​∑Var(Yi​)=nσ2​ and Var⁡(β^1)=σ2Sxx\operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta_1)=\frac{\sigma^2}{S_{xx}}Var(β^​1​)=Sxx​σ2​ (H25-11.6), so

    Var⁡(β^0)=σ2n+xˉ2σ2Sxx=σ2 Sxx+nxˉ2nSxx=∑i=1nxi2nSxxσ2,\operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta_0)=\frac{\sigma^2}{n}+\frac{\bar x^2\sigma^2}{S_{xx}}=\sigma^2\,\frac{S_{xx}+n\bar x^2}{nS_{xx}}=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^nx_i^2}{nS_{xx}}\sigma^2,Var(β^​0​)=nσ2​+Sxx​xˉ2σ2​=σ2nSxx​Sxx​+nxˉ2​=nSxx​∑i=1n​xi2​​σ2,

    because Sxx=∑xi2−2xˉ∑xi+nxˉ2=∑xi2−nxˉ2S_{xx}=\sum x_i^2-2\bar x\sum x_i+n\bar x^2=\sum x_i^2-n\bar x^2Sxx​=∑xi2​−2xˉ∑xi​+nxˉ2=∑xi2​−nxˉ2.

    Answer

    β^0∼N(β0, σ2∑xi2nSxx)\hat\beta_0\sim N\Big(\beta_0,\ \dfrac{\sigma^2\sum x_i^2}{nS_{xx}}\Big)β^​0​∼N(β0​, nSxx​σ2∑xi2​​), with Cov⁡(β^1,Yi)=xi−xˉSxxσ2\operatorname{Cov}(\hat\beta_1,Y_i)=\frac{x_i-\bar x}{S_{xx}}\sigma^2Cov(β^​1​,Yi​)=Sxx​xi​−xˉ​σ2 and Cov⁡(β^1,Yˉ)=0\operatorname{Cov}(\hat\beta_1,\bar Y)=0Cov(β^​1​,Yˉ)=0.

    BT9.18Unbiasedness, covariance and consistency of Θ^0,Θ^1\hat\Theta_0,\hat\Theta_1Θ^0​,Θ^1​ B&T Ch. 9 Problem 18*
    (Unbiasedness and consistency in linear regression.) In a probabilistic framework for regression, let us assume that Yi=θ0+θ1xi+WiY_i=\theta_0+\theta_1x_i+W_iYi​=θ0​+θ1​xi​+Wi​, i=1,…,ni=1,\dots,ni=1,…,n, where W1,…,WnW_1,\dots,W_nW1​,…,Wn​ are i.i.d. normal random variables with mean zero and variance σ2\sigma^2σ2. Then, given xix_ixi​ and the realized values yiy_iyi​ of YiY_iYi​, i=1,…,ni=1,\dots,ni=1,…,n, the ML estimates of θ0\theta_0θ0​ and θ1\theta_1θ1​ are given by the linear regression formulas.
    1. Show that the ML estimators Θ^0\hat\Theta_0Θ^0​ and Θ^1\hat\Theta_1Θ^1​ are unbiased.
    2. Show that the variances of the estimators Θ^0\hat\Theta_0Θ^0​ and Θ^1\hat\Theta_1Θ^1​ are var⁡(Θ^0)=σ2∑i=1nxi2n∑i=1n(xi−xˉ)2,var⁡(Θ^1)=σ2∑i=1n(xi−xˉ)2,\operatorname{var}(\hat\Theta_0)=\frac{\sigma^2\sum_{i=1}^nx_i^2}{n\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)^2},\qquad \operatorname{var}(\hat\Theta_1)=\frac{\sigma^2}{\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)^2},var(Θ^0​)=n∑i=1n​(xi​−xˉ)2σ2∑i=1n​xi2​​,var(Θ^1​)=∑i=1n​(xi​−xˉ)2σ2​, respectively, and their covariance is cov⁡(Θ^0,Θ^1)=−σ2xˉ∑i=1n(xi−xˉ)2\operatorname{cov}(\hat\Theta_0,\hat\Theta_1)=-\dfrac{\sigma^2\bar x}{\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)^2}cov(Θ^0​,Θ^1​)=−∑i=1n​(xi​−xˉ)2σ2xˉ​.
    3. Show that if ∑i=1n(xi−xˉ)2→∞\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)^2\to\infty∑i=1n​(xi​−xˉ)2→∞ and xˉ2\bar x^2xˉ2 is bounded by a constant as n→∞n\to\inftyn→∞, we have var⁡(Θ^0)→0\operatorname{var}(\hat\Theta_0)\to0var(Θ^0​)→0 and var⁡(Θ^1)→0\operatorname{var}(\hat\Theta_1)\to0var(Θ^1​)→0. (This, together with Chebyshev's inequality, implies that the estimators Θ^0\hat\Theta_0Θ^0​ and Θ^1\hat\Theta_1Θ^1​ are consistent.)

    Note: Although the assumption that the WiW_iWi​ are normal is needed for our estimators to be ML estimators, the argument shows that these estimators remain unbiased and consistent without this assumption.

    Solution · follows the B&T official solution

    (a) Unbiased

    Treat the xix_ixi​ as constants, write Sxx=∑(xi−xˉ)2S_{xx}=\sum(x_i-\bar x)^2Sxx​=∑(xi​−xˉ)2 and Wˉ=1n∑Wi\bar W=\frac1n\sum W_iWˉ=n1​∑Wi​. Then Yˉ=θ0+θ1xˉ+Wˉ\bar Y=\theta_0+\theta_1\bar x+\bar WYˉ=θ0​+θ1​xˉ+Wˉ, so Yi−Yˉ=θ1(xi−xˉ)+(Wi−Wˉ)Y_i-\bar Y=\theta_1(x_i-\bar x)+(W_i-\bar W)Yi​−Yˉ=θ1​(xi​−xˉ)+(Wi​−Wˉ) and

    Θ^1=∑(xi−xˉ)(Yi−Yˉ)Sxx=θ1+∑(xi−xˉ)(Wi−Wˉ)Sxx=θ1+∑i(xi−xˉ)WiSxx,\hat\Theta_1=\frac{\sum(x_i-\bar x)(Y_i-\bar Y)}{S_{xx}}=\theta_1+\frac{\sum(x_i-\bar x)(W_i-\bar W)}{S_{xx}}=\theta_1+\frac{\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)W_i}{S_{xx}},Θ^1​=Sxx​∑(xi​−xˉ)(Yi​−Yˉ)​=θ1​+Sxx​∑(xi​−xˉ)(Wi​−Wˉ)​=θ1​+Sxx​∑i​(xi​−xˉ)Wi​​,

    using ∑(xi−xˉ)=0\sum(x_i-\bar x)=0∑(xi​−xˉ)=0. Since E[Wi]=0E[W_i]=0E[Wi​]=0, E[Θ^1]=θ1E[\hat\Theta_1]=\theta_1E[Θ^1​]=θ1​. Also Θ^0=Yˉ−Θ^1xˉ=θ0+Wˉ−(Θ^1−θ1)xˉ\hat\Theta_0=\bar Y-\hat\Theta_1\bar x=\theta_0+\bar W-(\hat\Theta_1-\theta_1)\bar xΘ^0​=Yˉ−Θ^1​xˉ=θ0​+Wˉ−(Θ^1​−θ1​)xˉ, so E[Θ^0]=θ0+0−0=θ0E[\hat\Theta_0]=\theta_0+0-0=\theta_0E[Θ^0​]=θ0​+0−0=θ0​.

    (b) Variances and covariance

    From the formula in (a) and independence of the WiW_iWi​: var⁡(Θ^1)=∑(xi−xˉ)2σ2Sxx2=σ2Sxx\operatorname{var}(\hat\Theta_1)=\dfrac{\sum(x_i-\bar x)^2\sigma^2}{S_{xx}^2}=\dfrac{\sigma^2}{S_{xx}}var(Θ^1​)=Sxx2​∑(xi​−xˉ)2σ2​=Sxx​σ2​.

    Next, cov⁡(Wˉ,Θ^1)=1Sxx∑i(xi−xˉ)cov⁡(Wˉ,Wi)=σ2nSxx∑i(xi−xˉ)=0\operatorname{cov}(\bar W,\hat\Theta_1)=\dfrac{1}{S_{xx}}\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)\operatorname{cov}(\bar W,W_i)=\dfrac{\sigma^2}{nS_{xx}}\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)=0cov(Wˉ,Θ^1​)=Sxx​1​∑i​(xi​−xˉ)cov(Wˉ,Wi​)=nSxx​σ2​∑i​(xi​−xˉ)=0, since cov⁡(Wˉ,Wi)=σ2/n\operatorname{cov}(\bar W,W_i)=\sigma^2/ncov(Wˉ,Wi​)=σ2/n. With Θ^0=θ0+θ1xˉ+Wˉ−Θ^1xˉ\hat\Theta_0=\theta_0+\theta_1\bar x+\bar W-\hat\Theta_1\bar xΘ^0​=θ0​+θ1​xˉ+Wˉ−Θ^1​xˉ:

    4  Bayesian regression and linear LMS · slides 10–12, B&T §8.4

    Theory recap
    Gaussian prior gives penalised least squares (slides 10–11)

    Model the unknown coefficients by Θ0,Θ1\Theta_0,\Theta_1Θ0​,Θ1​ i.i.d. N(0,τ2)N(0,\tau^2)N(0,τ2); Gaussian noise as before. By Bayes' rule ln⁡fΘ∣Y(β0,β1∣y)=const−12σ2J(β0,β1)−β02+β122τ2,\ln f_{\Theta\mid Y}(\beta_0,\beta_1\mid y)=\text{const}-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}J(\beta_0,\beta_1)-\frac{\beta_0^2+\beta_1^2}{2\tau^2},lnfΘ∣Y​(β0​,β1​∣y)=const−2σ21​J(β0​,β1​)−2τ2β02​+β12​​, so, multiplying by −2σ2-2\sigma^2−2σ2, (β^0,β^1)MAP=arg⁡min⁡β0,β1[J(β0,β1)+λ(β02+β12)],λ=σ2τ2.(\hat\beta_0,\hat\beta_1)_{MAP}=\arg\min_{\beta_0,\beta_1}\Big[J(\beta_0,\beta_1)+\lambda(\beta_0^2+\beta_1^2)\Big],\qquad \lambda=\frac{\sigma^2}{\tau^2}.(β^​0​,β^​1​)MAP​=argβ0​,β1​min​[J(β0​,β1​)+λ(β02​+β12​)],λ=τ2σ2​. With centred inputs (xˉ=0\bar x=0xˉ=0) the two derivative equations are ∑iyi−nβ0=λβ0\sum_iy_i-n\beta_0=\lambda\beta_0∑i​yi​−nβ0​=λβ0​ and ∑ixiyi−β1∑ixi2=λβ1\sum_ix_iy_i-\beta_1\sum_ix_i^2=\lambda\beta_1∑i​xi​yi​−β1​∑i​xi2​=λβ1​, so β^0,MAP=∑iyin+λ,β^1,MAP=SxySxx+λ.\hat\beta_{0,MAP}=\frac{\sum_iy_i}{n+\lambda},\qquad \hat\beta_{1,MAP}=\frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}+\lambda}.β^​0,MAP​=n+λ∑i​yi​​,β^​1,MAP​=Sxx​+λSxy​​. Compared with ML (yˉ\bar yyˉ​ and Sxy/SxxS_{xy}/S_{xx}Sxy​/Sxx​), the prior adds λ\lambdaλ to each denominator: shrinkage towards 0. With λ=1\lambda=1λ=1, β^0,MAP=∑yi/(n+1)\hat\beta_{0,MAP}=\sum y_i/(n+1)β^​0,MAP​=∑yi​/(n+1), the Gaussian-prior example of L23–24 with μ0=0\mu_0=0μ0​=0.

    Posterior and CE estimate (slide 12)

    Completing the square, given Y=yY=yY=y: Θ0∼N(m0,v0)\Theta_0\sim N(m_0,v_0)Θ0​∼N(m0​,v0​), Θ1∼N(m1,v1)\Theta_1\sim N(m_1,v_1)Θ1​∼N(m1​,v1​), independent, with m0=∑iyin+λ,v0=σ2n+λ,m1=SxySxx+λ,v1=σ2Sxx+λ.m_0=\frac{\sum_iy_i}{n+\lambda},\quad v_0=\frac{\sigma^2}{n+\lambda},\qquad m_1=\frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}+\lambda},\quad v_1=\frac{\sigma^2}{S_{xx}+\lambda}.m0​=n+λ∑i​yi​​,v0​=n+λσ2​,m1​=Sxx​+λSxy​​,v1​=Sxx​+λσ2​. For a Gaussian the mode equals the mean, so β^j,CE=E[Θj∣Y=y]=mj=β^j,MAP\hat\beta_{j,CE}=E[\Theta_j\mid Y=y]=m_j=\hat\beta_{j,MAP}β^​j,CE​=E[Θj​∣Y=y]=mj​=β^​j,MAP​.

    Linear LMS (B&T §8.4; beyond the slides)

    Among estimators aX+ba X+baX+b, the one minimising E[(Θ−aX−b)2]E[(\Theta-aX-b)^2]E[(Θ−aX−b)2] is Θ^L=E[Θ]+cov⁡(Θ,X)var⁡(X)(X−E[X]),E[(Θ−Θ^L)2]=(1−ρ2)var⁡(Θ).\hat\Theta_L=E[\Theta]+\frac{\operatorname{cov}(\Theta,X)}{\operatorname{var}(X)}\big(X-E[X]\big),\qquad E\big[(\Theta-\hat\Theta_L)^2\big]=(1-\rho^2)\operatorname{var}(\Theta).Θ^L​=E[Θ]+var(X)cov(Θ,X)​(X−E[X]),E[(Θ−Θ^L​)2]=(1−ρ2)var(Θ). Derivation: for fixed aaa, the best bbb is E[Θ]−aE[X]E[\Theta]-aE[X]E[Θ]−aE[X]; then minimise var⁡(Θ−aX)=var⁡Θ−2acov⁡(Θ,X)+a2var⁡X\operatorname{var}(\Theta-aX)=\operatorname{var}\Theta-2a\operatorname{cov}(\Theta,X)+a^2\operatorname{var}Xvar(Θ−aX)=varΘ−2acov(Θ,X)+a2varX in aaa. The error is uncorrelated with XXX (orthogonality). Regression is the sample version: replace cov/var by Sxy/SxxS_{xy}/S_{xx}Sxy​/Sxx​ and the means by xˉ,yˉ\bar x,\bar yxˉ,yˉ​ and you get β^1,β^0\hat\beta_1,\hat\beta_0β^​1​,β^​0​ (PC §8.5.2). With several observations, set every partial derivative of the MSE to zero (a system of linear equations).

    When the estimators agree

    If E[Θ∣X]E[\Theta\mid X]E[Θ∣X] happens to be linear in XXX (e.g. jointly Gaussian Θ,X\Theta,XΘ,X), it is also the linear LMS estimator; if the posterior is also symmetric and unimodal, the MAP estimate is the same point. Slide 12 is one instance: Gaussian posterior, CE = MAP.

    Watch out

    Linear LMS needs only means, variances and covariances, never the full distribution. A zero covariance makes it ignore the data (BT8.17); a transformed observation may help.

    BT8.17Estimating a variance: use X2X^2X2, not XXX B&T Ch. 8 Problem 17
    Let Θ\ThetaΘ be a positive random variable, with known mean μ\muμ and variance σ2\sigma^2σ2, to be estimated on the basis of a measurement XXX of the form X=Θ WX=\sqrt\Theta\,WX=Θ​W. We assume that WWW is independent of Θ\ThetaΘ with zero mean, unit variance, and known fourth moment E[W4]E[W^4]E[W4]. Thus, the conditional mean and variance of XXX given Θ\ThetaΘ are 0 and Θ\ThetaΘ, respectively, so we are essentially trying to estimate the variance of XXX given an observed value. Find the linear LMS estimator of Θ\ThetaΘ based on XXX, and the linear LMS estimator of Θ\ThetaΘ based on X2X^2X2.
    Solution · follows the B&T official solution

    Based on XXX

    By independence, E[X]=E[Θ]E[W]=0E[X]=E[\sqrt\Theta]E[W]=0E[X]=E[Θ​]E[W]=0 and cov⁡(Θ,X)=E[ΘX]−E[Θ]E[X]=E[Θ3/2]E[W]−0=0\operatorname{cov}(\Theta,X)=E[\Theta X]-E[\Theta]E[X]=E[\Theta^{3/2}]E[W]-0=0cov(Θ,X)=E[ΘX]−E[Θ]E[X]=E[Θ3/2]E[W]−0=0. So the slope is 0 and Θ^=E[Θ]=μ\hat\Theta=E[\Theta]=\muΘ^=E[Θ]=μ: the linear LMS estimator ignores XXX.

    Based on Y=X2=ΘW2Y=X^2=\Theta W^2Y=X2=ΘW2

    E[Y]=E[Θ]E[W2]=μ,E[ΘY]=E[Θ2]E[W2]=σ2+μ2,cov⁡(Θ,Y)=σ2+μ2−μ⋅μ=σ2,E[Y]=E[\Theta]E[W^2]=\mu,\qquad E[\Theta Y]=E[\Theta^2]E[W^2]=\sigma^2+\mu^2,\qquad \operatorname{cov}(\Theta,Y)=\sigma^2+\mu^2-\mu\cdot\mu=\sigma^2,E[Y]=E[Θ]E[W2]=μ,E[ΘY]=E[Θ2]E[W2]=σ2+μ2,cov(Θ,Y)=σ2+μ2−μ⋅μ=σ2, var⁡(Y)=E[Θ2W4]−(E[Y])2=(σ2+μ2)E[W4]−μ2.\operatorname{var}(Y)=E[\Theta^2W^4]-(E[Y])^2=(\sigma^2+\mu^2)E[W^4]-\mu^2 .var(Y)=E[Θ2W4]−(E[Y])2=(σ2+μ2)E[W4]−μ2. Θ^=μ+σ2(σ2+μ2)E[W4]−μ2 (X2−μ).\hat\Theta=\mu+\frac{\sigma^2}{(\sigma^2+\mu^2)E[W^4]-\mu^2}\,\big(X^2-\mu\big).Θ^=μ+(σ2+μ2)E[W4]−μ2σ2​(X2−μ).

    Its MSE is σ2−σ4(σ2+μ2)E[W4]−μ2<σ2\sigma^2-\dfrac{\sigma^4}{(\sigma^2+\mu^2)E[W^4]-\mu^2}<\sigma^2σ2−(σ2+μ2)E[W4]−μ2σ4​<σ2: the transformed observation helps. A large X2X^2X2 suggests a large variance Θ\ThetaΘ.

    Typo in the official solution

    The solution manual prints the last factor as (Y−σ2)(Y-\sigma^2)(Y−σ2); it must be (Y−E[Y])=(X2−μ)(Y-E[Y])=(X^2-\mu)(Y−E[Y])=(X2−μ).

    BT8.19Photon counts: linear LMS of the transmitted number B&T Ch. 8 Problem 19
    Consider a photodetector in an optical communications system that counts the number of photons arriving during a certain interval. A user conveys information by switching a photon transmitter on or off. Assume that the probability of the transmitter being on is ppp. If the transmitter is on, the number of photons transmitted over the interval of interest is a Poisson random variable Θ\ThetaΘ with mean λ\lambdaλ. If the transmitter is off, the number of photons transmitted is zero. Unfortunately, regardless of whether or not the transmitter is on or off, photons may still be detected due to a phenomenon called "shot noise." The number NNN of detected shot noise photons is a Poisson random variable with mean μ\muμ. Thus, the total number XXX of detected photons is equal to Θ+N\Theta+NΘ+N if the transmitter is on, and is equal to NNN otherwise. We assume that NNN and Θ\ThetaΘ are independent, so that Θ+N\Theta+NΘ+N is also Poisson with mean λ+μ\lambda+\muλ+μ.
    1. What is the probability that the transmitter was on, given that the photodetector detected kkk photons?
    2. Describe the MAP rule for deciding whether the transmitter was on.
    3. Find the linear LMS estimator of the number of transmitted photons, based on the number of detected photons.

    (The book has no part (b). Part (d) is this topic's question; (a) and (c) are Bayes/MAP, done briefly.)

    Solution · follows the B&T official solution

    (a)

    P(on∣X=k)=p (λ+μ)ke−(λ+μ)k!p (λ+μ)ke−(λ+μ)k!+(1−p)μke−μk!=p(λ+μ)ke−λp(λ+μ)ke−λ+(1−p)μk.P(\text{on}\mid X=k)=\frac{p\,\frac{(\lambda+\mu)^ke^{-(\lambda+\mu)}}{k!}}{p\,\frac{(\lambda+\mu)^ke^{-(\lambda+\mu)}}{k!}+(1-p)\frac{\mu^ke^{-\mu}}{k!}}=\frac{p(\lambda+\mu)^ke^{-\lambda}}{p(\lambda+\mu)^ke^{-\lambda}+(1-p)\mu^k}.P(on∣X=k)=pk!(λ+μ)ke−(λ+μ)​+(1−p)k!μke−μ​pk!(λ+μ)ke−(λ+μ)​​=p(λ+μ)ke−λ+(1−p)μkp(λ+μ)ke−λ​.

    (c)

    Decide "on" iff this posterior is at least 1/21/21/2, i.e. iff p(λ+μ)ke−λ≥(1−p)μkp(\lambda+\mu)^ke^{-\lambda}\ge(1-p)\mu^kp(λ+μ)ke−λ≥(1−p)μk.

    (d) Linear LMS

    Let SSS be the number transmitted: S=ΘS=\ThetaS=Θ with probability ppp, S=0S=0S=0 otherwise; X=S+NX=S+NX=S+N with S,NS,NS,N independent. S^=E[S]+cov⁡(S,X)σX2(X−E[X])\hat S=E[S]+\frac{\operatorname{cov}(S,X)}{\sigma_X^2}(X-E[X])S^=E[S]+σX2​cov(S,X)​(X−E[X]), with

    E[S]=pλ,E[S2]=pE[Θ2]=p(λ2+λ),σS2=p(λ2+λ)−p2λ2=pλ+p(1−p)λ2,E[S]=p\lambda,\quad E[S^2]=pE[\Theta^2]=p(\lambda^2+\lambda),\quad \sigma_S^2=p(\lambda^2+\lambda)-p^2\lambda^2=p\lambda+p(1-p)\lambda^2,E[S]=pλ,E[S2]=pE[Θ2]=p(λ2+λ),σS2​=p(λ2+λ)−p2λ2=pλ+p(1−p)λ2, E[X]=pλ+μ,σX2=σS2+σN2=pλ+μ+p(1−p)λ2,E[X]=p\lambda+\mu,\qquad \sigma_X^2=\sigma_S^2+\sigma_N^2=p\lambda+\mu+p(1-p)\lambda^2,E[X]=pλ+μ,σX2​=σS2​+σN2​=pλ+μ+p(1−p)λ2, cov⁡(S,X)=cov⁡(S,S+N)=σS2+cov⁡(S,N)=σS2(S,N independent).\operatorname{cov}(S,X)=\operatorname{cov}(S,S+N)=\sigma_S^2+\operatorname{cov}(S,N)=\sigma_S^2\quad(S,N\ \text{independent}).cov(S,X)=cov(S,S+N)=σS2​+cov(S,N)=σS2​(S,N independent).

    BT8.20Spherically invariant PDFs: MAP = LMS = linear LMS B&T Ch. 8 Problem 20*
    (Estimation with spherically invariant PDFs.) Let Θ\ThetaΘ and XXX be continuous random variables with joint PDF of the form fΘ,X(θ,x)=h(q(θ,x))f_{\Theta,X}(\theta,x)=h(q(\theta,x))fΘ,X​(θ,x)=h(q(θ,x)), where hhh is a nonnegative scalar function, and q(θ,x)q(\theta,x)q(θ,x) is a quadratic function of the form q(θ,x)=a(θ−θˉ)2+b(x−xˉ)2−2c(θ−θˉ)(x−xˉ).q(\theta,x)=a(\theta-\bar\theta)^2+b(x-\bar x)^2-2c(\theta-\bar\theta)(x-\bar x).q(θ,x)=a(θ−θˉ)2+b(x−xˉ)2−2c(θ−θˉ)(x−xˉ). Here a,b,c,θˉ,xˉa,b,c,\bar\theta,\bar xa,b,c,θˉ,xˉ are some scalars with a≠0a\neq0a=0. Derive the LMS and linear LMS estimates, for any xxx such that E[Θ∣X=x]E[\Theta\mid X=x]E[Θ∣X=x] is well-defined and finite. Assuming that q(θ,x)≥0q(\theta,x)\ge0q(θ,x)≥0 for all x,θx,\thetax,θ, and that hhh is monotonically decreasing, derive the MAP estimate and show that it coincides with the LMS and linear LMS estimates.
    Solution · follows the B&T official solution

    Complete the square in θ\thetaθ. With θ∗(x)=θˉ+ca(x−xˉ)\theta^*(x)=\bar\theta+\frac ca(x-\bar x)θ∗(x)=θˉ+ac​(x−xˉ),

    q(θ,x)=a(θ−θ∗(x))2+(b−c2a)(x−xˉ)2.q(\theta,x)=a\big(\theta-\theta^*(x)\big)^2+\Big(b-\frac{c^2}{a}\Big)(x-\bar x)^2 .q(θ,x)=a(θ−θ∗(x))2+(b−ac2​)(x−xˉ)2.

    (Expand: a(θ−θˉ)2−2c(θ−θˉ)(x−xˉ)+c2a(x−xˉ)2a(\theta-\bar\theta)^2-2c(\theta-\bar\theta)(x-\bar x)+\frac{c^2}{a}(x-\bar x)^2a(θ−θˉ)2−2c(θ−θˉ)(x−xˉ)+ac2​(x−xˉ)2 is the first term.)

    LMS. For fixed xxx, the posterior fΘ∣X(θ∣x)=h(q(θ,x))/fX(x)f_{\Theta\mid X}(\theta\mid x)=h(q(\theta,x))/f_X(x)fΘ∣X​(θ∣x)=h(q(θ,x))/fX​(x) depends on θ\thetaθ only through (θ−θ∗(x))2(\theta-\theta^*(x))^2(θ−θ∗(x))2, so it is symmetric about θ∗(x)\theta^*(x)θ∗(x). A symmetric density with a finite mean has its mean at the centre of symmetry:

    E[Θ∣X=x]=θ∗(x)=θˉ+ca(x−xˉ).E[\Theta\mid X=x]=\theta^*(x)=\bar\theta+\frac ca(x-\bar x).E[Θ∣X=x]=θ∗(x)=θˉ+ac​(x−xˉ).

    Linear LMS. The LMS estimator has the smallest MSE among all estimators, and here it is linear in xxx; so no linear estimator does better and the linear LMS estimator is the same, θˉ+ca(X−xˉ)\bar\theta+\frac ca(X-\bar x)θˉ+ac​(X−xˉ).

    MAP. If q≥0q\ge0q≥0 everywhere then a>0a>0a>0 (take x=xˉx=\bar xx=xˉ). Since hhh is decreasing, maximising h(q(θ,x))h(q(\theta,x))h(q(θ,x)) over θ\thetaθ means minimising q(θ,x)q(\theta,x)q(θ,x), and ∂q/∂θ=2a(θ−θˉ)−2c(x−xˉ)=0\partial q/\partial\theta=2a(\theta-\bar\theta)-2c(x-\bar x)=0∂q/∂θ=2a(θ−θˉ)−2c(x−xˉ)=0 gives θ=θ∗(x)\theta=\theta^*(x)θ=θ∗(x), a minimum because a>0a>0a>0. So all three coincide.

    This is the mechanism behind slide 12: a bivariate Gaussian has this form (h(q)∝e−q/2h(q)\propto e^{-q/2}h(q)∝e−q/2), so its CE and MAP estimates coincide and are linear.

    Answer

    θ^MAP=E[Θ∣X=x]=θ^L=θˉ+ca(x−xˉ)\hat\theta_{MAP}=E[\Theta\mid X=x]=\hat\theta_{L}=\bar\theta+\dfrac ca(x-\bar x)θ^MAP​=E[Θ∣X=x]=θ^L​=θˉ+ac​(x−xˉ).

    BT8.21Linear LMS from two observations B&T Ch. 8 Problem 21*
    (Linear LMS estimation based on two observations.) Consider three random variables Θ\ThetaΘ, XXX, and YYY, with known variances and covariances. Assume that var⁡(X)>0\operatorname{var}(X)>0var(X)>0, var⁡(Y)>0\operatorname{var}(Y)>0var(Y)>0, and that ∣ρ(X,Y)∣≠1|\rho(X,Y)|\neq1∣ρ(X,Y)∣=1. Give a formula for the linear LMS estimator of Θ\ThetaΘ based on XXX and YYY, assuming that XXX and YYY are uncorrelated, and also in the general case.
    Solution · follows the B&T official solution

    Look for Θ^=aX+bY+c\hat\Theta=aX+bY+cΘ^=aX+bY+c minimising E[(Θ−aX−bY−c)2]E[(\Theta-aX-bY-c)^2]E[(Θ−aX−bY−c)2]. For fixed a,ba,ba,b this is minimised by c=E[Θ]−aE[X]−bE[Y]c=E[\Theta]-aE[X]-bE[Y]c=E[Θ]−aE[X]−bE[Y] (best constant = mean), which leaves E[((Θ−EΘ)−a(X−EX)−b(Y−EY))2]E\big[\big((\Theta-E\Theta)-a(X-EX)-b(Y-EY)\big)^2\big]E[((Θ−EΘ)−a(X−EX)−b(Y−EY))2]. So assume zero means and add them back at the end. Then

    E[(Θ−aX−bY)2]=E[Θ2]+a2E[X2]+b2E[Y2]−2aE[ΘX]−2bE[ΘY]+2abE[XY].E[(\Theta-aX-bY)^2]=E[\Theta^2]+a^2E[X^2]+b^2E[Y^2]-2aE[\Theta X]-2bE[\Theta Y]+2abE[XY].E[(Θ−aX−bY)2]=E[Θ2]+a2E[X2]+b2E[Y2]−2aE[ΘX]−2bE[ΘY]+2abE[XY].

    Set the partial derivatives to zero:

    avar⁡(X)+bcov⁡(X,Y)=cov⁡(Θ,X),acov⁡(X,Y)+bvar⁡(Y)=cov⁡(Θ,Y).a\operatorname{var}(X)+b\operatorname{cov}(X,Y)=\operatorname{cov}(\Theta,X),\qquad a\operatorname{cov}(X,Y)+b\operatorname{var}(Y)=\operatorname{cov}(\Theta,Y).avar(X)+bcov(X,Y)=cov(Θ,X),acov(X,Y)+bvar(Y)=cov(Θ,Y).

    The determinant var⁡Xvar⁡Y−cov⁡2(X,Y)=var⁡Xvar⁡Y(1−ρ2)>0\operatorname{var}X\operatorname{var}Y-\operatorname{cov}^2(X,Y)=\operatorname{var}X\operatorname{var}Y(1-\rho^2)>0varXvarY−cov2(X,Y)=varXvarY(1−ρ2)>0 because ∣ρ∣≠1|\rho|\neq1∣ρ∣=1, so (Cramer's rule)

    a=var⁡(Y)cov⁡(Θ,X)−cov⁡(Θ,Y)cov⁡(X,Y)var⁡(X)var⁡(Y)−cov⁡2(X,Y),b=var⁡(X)cov⁡(Θ,Y)−cov⁡(Θ,X)cov⁡(X,Y)var⁡(X)var⁡(Y)−cov⁡2(X,Y).a=\frac{\operatorname{var}(Y)\operatorname{cov}(\Theta,X)-\operatorname{cov}(\Theta,Y)\operatorname{cov}(X,Y)}{\operatorname{var}(X)\operatorname{var}(Y)-\operatorname{cov}^2(X,Y)},\qquad b=\frac{\operatorname{var}(X)\operatorname{cov}(\Theta,Y)-\operatorname{cov}(\Theta,X)\operatorname{cov}(X,Y)}{\operatorname{var}(X)\operatorname{var}(Y)-\operatorname{cov}^2(X,Y)}.a=var(X)var(Y)−cov2(X,Y)var(Y)cov(Θ,X)−cov(Θ,Y)cov(X,Y)​,b=var(X)var(Y)−cov2(X,Y)var(X)cov(Θ,Y)−cov(Θ,X)cov(X,Y)​.

    The MSE is a convex quadratic in (a,b)(a,b)(a,b) (its Hessian is twice the covariance matrix of (X,Y)(X,Y)(X,Y), positive definite), so this stationary point is the minimum. If cov⁡(X,Y)=0\operatorname{cov}(X,Y)=0cov(X,Y)=0: a=cov⁡(Θ,X)/var⁡Xa=\operatorname{cov}(\Theta,X)/\operatorname{var}Xa=cov(Θ,X)/varX, b=cov⁡(Θ,Y)/var⁡Yb=\operatorname{cov}(\Theta,Y)/\operatorname{var}Yb=cov(Θ,Y)/varY.

    Answer

    Uncorrelated: Θ^=E[Θ]+cov⁡(Θ,X)var⁡X(X−E[X])+cov⁡(Θ,Y)var⁡Y(Y−E[Y])\hat\Theta=E[\Theta]+\frac{\operatorname{cov}(\Theta,X)}{\operatorname{var}X}(X-E[X])+\frac{\operatorname{cov}(\Theta,Y)}{\operatorname{var}Y}(Y-E[Y])Θ^=E[Θ]+varXcov(Θ,X)​(X−E[X])+varYcov(Θ,Y)​(Y−E[Y]). General: Θ^=E[Θ]+a(X−E[X])+b(Y−E[Y])\hat\Theta=E[\Theta]+a(X-E[X])+b(Y-E[Y])Θ^=E[Θ]+a(X−E[X])+b(Y−E[Y]) with a,ba,ba,b above (checked numerically against a matrix solve).

    BT8.22Linear LMS from nnn noisy measurements B&T Ch. 8 Problem 22*
    (Linear LMS estimation based on multiple observations.) Let Θ\ThetaΘ be a random variable with mean μ\muμ and variance σ02\sigma_0^2σ02​, and let X1,…,XnX_1,\dots,X_nX1​,…,Xn​ be observations of the form Xi=Θ+WiX_i=\Theta+W_iXi​=Θ+Wi​, where the observation errors WiW_iWi​ are random variables with mean 0 and variance σi2\sigma_i^2σi2​. We assume that the random variables Θ,W1,…,Wn\Theta,W_1,\dots,W_nΘ,W1​,…,Wn​ are independent. Verify that the linear LMS estimator of Θ\ThetaΘ based on X1,…,XnX_1,\dots,X_nX1​,…,Xn​ is Θ^=μ/σ02+∑i=1nXi/σi2∑i=0n1/σi2,\hat\Theta=\frac{\mu/\sigma_0^2+\sum_{i=1}^nX_i/\sigma_i^2}{\sum_{i=0}^n1/\sigma_i^2},Θ^=∑i=0n​1/σi2​μ/σ02​+∑i=1n​Xi​/σi2​​, by minimizing over a1,…,an,ba_1,\dots,a_n,ba1​,…,an​,b the function h(a1,…,an,b)=E[(Θ−a1X1−⋯−anXn−b)2]h(a_1,\dots,a_n,b)=E\big[(\Theta-a_1X_1-\cdots-a_nX_n-b)^2\big]h(a1​,…,an​,b)=E[(Θ−a1​X1​−⋯−an​Xn​−b)2].
    Solution · follows the B&T official solution

    Let A=1−∑iaiA=1-\sum_ia_iA=1−∑i​ai​. Then Θ−∑iaiXi−b=AΘ−∑iaiWi−b\Theta-\sum_ia_iX_i-b=A\Theta-\sum_ia_iW_i-bΘ−∑i​ai​Xi​−b=AΘ−∑i​ai​Wi​−b. The WiW_iWi​ have mean 0 and are independent of each other and of Θ\ThetaΘ, so the cross terms vanish:

    h=A2E[Θ2]−2Abμ+b2+∑iai2σi2=A2σ02+(Aμ−b)2+∑i=1nai2σi2.h=A^2E[\Theta^2]-2Ab\mu+b^2+\sum_ia_i^2\sigma_i^2=A^2\sigma_0^2+(A\mu-b)^2+\sum_{i=1}^na_i^2\sigma_i^2 .h=A2E[Θ2]−2Abμ+b2+i∑​ai2​σi2​=A2σ02​+(Aμ−b)2+i=1∑n​ai2​σi2​.

    hhh is a sum of squares in the unknowns, hence convex; a stationary point is the minimum.

    ∂h∂b=−2(Aμ−b)=0⇒b=Aμ;∂h∂aj=−2Aσ02−2μ(Aμ−b)+2ajσj2=0⇒aj=Aσ02σj2.\frac{\partial h}{\partial b}=-2(A\mu-b)=0\Rightarrow b=A\mu;\qquad \frac{\partial h}{\partial a_j}=-2A\sigma_0^2-2\mu(A\mu-b)+2a_j\sigma_j^2=0\Rightarrow a_j=\frac{A\sigma_0^2}{\sigma_j^2}.∂b∂h​=−2(Aμ−b)=0⇒b=Aμ;∂aj​∂h​=−2Aσ02​−2μ(Aμ−b)+2aj​σj2​=0⇒aj​=σj2​Aσ02​​.

    Substitute into A=1−∑jaj=1−Aσ02∑j≥11/σj2A=1-\sum_ja_j=1-A\sigma_0^2\sum_{j\ge1}1/\sigma_j^2A=1−∑j​aj​=1−Aσ02​∑j≥1​1/σj2​:

    A=11+σ02∑j=1n1/σj2=1/σ02D,D=∑i=0n1σi2,aj=1/σj2D,b=μ/σ02D.A=\frac{1}{1+\sigma_0^2\sum_{j=1}^n1/\sigma_j^2}=\frac{1/\sigma_0^2}{D},\qquad D=\sum_{i=0}^n\frac{1}{\sigma_i^2},\qquad a_j=\frac{1/\sigma_j^2}{D},\qquad b=\frac{\mu/\sigma_0^2}{D}.A=1+σ02​∑j=1n​1/σj2​1​=D1/σ02​​,D=i=0∑n​σi2​1​,aj​=D1/σj2​​,b=Dμ/σ02​​.

    So Θ^=∑jajXj+b=μ/σ02+∑jXj/σj2D\hat\Theta=\sum_ja_jX_j+b=\dfrac{\mu/\sigma_0^2+\sum_jX_j/\sigma_j^2}{D}Θ^=∑j​aj​Xj​+b=Dμ/σ02​+∑j​Xj​/σj2​​: a precision-weighted average of the prior mean and the measurements. Its MSE is h=A2σ02+∑jaj2σj2=1/σ02+∑j1/σj2D2=1Dh=A^2\sigma_0^2+\sum_ja_j^2\sigma_j^2=\frac{1/\sigma_0^2+\sum_j1/\sigma_j^2}{D^2}=\frac1Dh=A2σ02​+∑j​aj2​σj2​=D21/σ02​+∑j​1/σj2​​=D1​ (checked symbolically).

    Link to the lecture: with all variances equal to σ2\sigma^2σ2, Θ^=μ+∑Xin+1\hat\Theta=\frac{\mu+\sum X_i}{n+1}Θ^=n+1μ+∑Xi​​ with MSE σ2n+1\frac{\sigma^2}{n+1}n+1σ2​, exactly the posterior mean and variance of the Gaussian-prior example (slide 11 with μ0=0\mu_0=0μ0​=0). For Gaussian Θ,Wi\Theta,W_iΘ,Wi​ the CE estimate is linear, so CE = MAP = linear LMS.

    Answer

    aj=1/σj2∑i=0n1/σi2, b=μ/σ02∑i=0n1/σi2a_j=\dfrac{1/\sigma_j^2}{\sum_{i=0}^n1/\sigma_i^2},\ b=\dfrac{\mu/\sigma_0^2}{\sum_{i=0}^n1/\sigma_i^2}aj​=∑i=0n​1/σi2​1/σj2​​, b=∑i=0n​1/σi2​μ/σ02​​, giving the stated Θ^\hat\ThetaΘ^; MSE =1/∑i=0nσi−2=1/\sum_{i=0}^n\sigma_i^{-2}=1/∑i=0n​σi−2​.
